Stage dancers and movie stars love to wear the feather version of me around their necks.

media.credit: Olympic National Park · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Olympic National Park

questions.fun_fact: In “The Little Prince”, the very first drawing shows a boa that swallowed an elephant, though grown-ups think it's a hat.

quality.notes: The feather-boa clue works in Spanish and German too ('boa de plumas', 'Federboa'). Pythons and anacondas also have no venom and squeeze their prey, so only the scarf clue singles out the boa. That is fine but means the riddle rests on one clue. q-1624 asks about the same animal but a different fact (where it lives). The Little Prince fun fact is a nice touch.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which translated the answer's name, with a hint about live birth.

hints: I live in the forests of Central and South America.
My second name means “the squeezer”.
Stage dancers and movie stars love to wear the feather version of me around their necks.

questions.description: The game that kept office computers busy while their owners were supposed to be working.

media.author: Kskhh

quality.notes: 'Solitaire' can also mean the peg board game (in British English the card game is often called 'patience'). The Windows context and the options make the card game clear. q-5400 also has playing cards as the answer, but it asks a different thing.

questions.description: A fancy word that makes frogs sound like secret agents.

hints: It has to do with the time of day.

When you go to bed, they wake up.

media.author: Alan Hughes

questions.fun_fact: Many frogs have huge eyes that help them see well in the dark.

media.author: Masato Ohta from Tokyo, Japan.

media.author: Andrew Braun

hints: You often eat it with chopsticks.
It's long and thin.
Ramen is a famous kind of it.

questions.description: Tiles, fountains and orange trees: Seville is showing off again.

Kings and queens live in buildings like this.

media.author: Jebulon

questions.fun_fact: The Alcázar of Seville is one of the oldest royal palaces in Europe still in use, and its gardens appeared in “Game of Thrones”.

quality.notes: 'Oldest royal palace still in use' is commonly claimed but hard to check exactly. The question is a little dry, and Seville is a Spain-focused subject. 'Mosque' is a fair distractor.

review.feedback: The clue is the answer's own name: "alcázar" is an everyday Spanish word (from Arabic al-qasr) meaning a fortified palace, and in Spanish the building is the "Real Alcázar", literally "royal palace". So the question collapses in the Spanish versions. Hints 1 ("built it for rulers") and 2 ("thrones") also rule out all three wrong answers straight away.

questions.description: Columns standing in a neat row, like guests waiting to get in.

questions.description: Patterns so twisty they could make a carpet dizzy.

revision.reason: Rewrote hints 1 and 2 so together they no longer leave only plants.

hints: In mosques, the art rarely shows people or animals.

questions.description: A 1982 game box that badly wanted to be the coolest kid on the block.

An add-on let it play Atari 2600 games
Its controllers had a phone-style number pad
hints: Three of these really helped it sell in the early 1980s.
One of the true facts came from a deal with a famous Japanese game company.
The maker's name came from a small state in New England.

media.credit: Ziko van Dijk · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ziko van Dijk

questions.fun_fact: Coleco began as the Connecticut Leather Company, selling leather supplies to shoemakers.

quality.notes: All the facts check out: Coleco was the Connecticut Leather Company, Donkey Kong came packed with the console, Expansion Module #1 played Atari 2600 games and the controllers had keypads. The fact is very niche, close to 15. A 'NOT true' question about one console feels like a dry spec sheet. The 'retro game console 1980s' query could turn up a ColecoVision photo, which doesn't give the answer away but is worth knowing. Hint 2 points at the non-toy origin, so it narrows things down a lot.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which pointed at the only option about the maker, with a hint about a true fact.

hints: Three of these really helped it sell in the early 1980s.

The maker's name came from a small state in New England.

questions.description: Before electricity, rivers had a day job too.

media.author: Alpsdake

questions.description: For families who think every picnic needs a life jacket.

questions.description: A good dog that has never once chewed a shoe.

questions.description: A video game where the guitar solo is mightier than the sword, and much louder.

questions.description: Long before the stadium guitar heroes, someone was already shredding in church.

questions.description: An album cover so mysterious it forgot to say who made it.

questions.description: An emperor who made it big in Rome but never forgot his hometown.

The country's capital is Tripoli.

media.author: Syed Wali Peeran

questions.description: The only wishing well with its own sea god and a very busy cleaning crew.

hints: The fountain's main statue shows the sea god Oceanus.

media.author: Dennis G. Jarvis

hints: You can often find one in your kitchen or fridge.
A cork keeps the water out.
You could also drink juice from it before using it this way.

media.credit: Daniel Ramirez from Honolulu, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daniel Ramirez from Honolulu, USA

questions.fun_fact: In 2018, a message in a bottle found on an Australian beach turned out to have been thrown from a German ship 132 years earlier.

quality.notes: Fun fact checks out: the Wedge Island bottle from 1886, found in 2018.

questions.description: Time flies, they say, but on old sailing ships it mostly trickled.
questions.question: I have two glass bulbs joined in the middle, and sand trickles from the top one to the bottom one. Sailors used me to measure time. What am I?
hints: When all the sand has fallen, you turn me upside down.
Some board games use a small one to time each turn.
My name tells you how much time I often measure.

media.credit: Hendrick Cornelisz Vroom · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hendrick Cornelisz Vroom

questions.fun_fact: On old ships, a sailor turned a half-hour glass all day and night and rang the ship's bell each time, which is how the crew kept track of time.

quality.notes: The distractors are weak: only one option has sand or bulbs, so the riddle settles it right away. That's fine at this level.

questions.description: A chilly finish line where the race to get there first made headlines around the world.
questions.question: It sits on ice almost 3 km (2 miles) thick, it's colder than almost anywhere else, and explorers first reached it in 1911. What is it?
hints: It's at one end of the line Earth spins around.
No country owns the land around it, and scientists live there in research stations.
It's in the middle of Antarctica.

media.credit: owamux · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: owamux

questions.fun_fact: Roald Amundsen's team from Norway reached it on December 14, 1911, beating Robert Falcon Scott's team by about five weeks.

quality.notes: The only real clues that separate South from North Pole are "thick ice" (the North Pole sits on thin floating sea ice) and "1911". Young kids won't know either, so 2 is underrated; it's closer to 5. Its structure is close to the North Pole question q-4229, but the fact asked is different.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which named Antarctica, with a vaguer clue, and moved the Antarctica clue to hint 3.

hints: It's at one end of the line Earth spins around.
It's in the middle of Antarctica.
It's the opposite of where Santa is said to live.

questions.description: It makes you sneeze, and once upon a time it kept merchants very, very busy.
questions.question: In medieval Europe, pepper came from far away, it was rare, and it cost a fortune. So what did people sometimes use it as?
hints: Think about why something rare and costly is useful.
Merchants guarded it in locked chests, like treasure.
Today you'd use coins or bills for the same job.

media.credit: Xitop753 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Xitop753

questions.fun_fact: When Alaric's army besieged Rome in 408, part of the ransom he demanded was 3,000 pounds of pepper.

quality.notes: "Rare and cost a fortune" points straight at money, and paint, glue and lamp fuel are weak against it. Hint 2 ("pay your rent") nearly gives the answer away. Calling pepper used "as money" is a slight simplification, but it's well attested (peppercorn rents, Alaric's ransom).

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which described paying with money, with a vaguer treasure hint.

hints: Think about why something rare and costly is useful.
You could pay your rent with it.
Today you'd use coins or bills for the same job.

questions.description: Royal robes, fancy ties and pajamas fit for a queen, all thanks to a secret China guarded for centuries.
questions.question: This soft, shiny cloth was first made in ancient China. Which animal spins the thread for it?
hints: Ancient China kept this animal's work a secret for a very long time.
It's a caterpillar that eats mulberry leaves.
It wraps itself in a cocoon made of one long thread.

media.note: A clear photo of shiny silk cloth or rolls of silk fabric, with no animals or cocoons visible.

questions.fun_fact: A single silkworm cocoon is made from one thread that can be up to about 900 m (almost 3,000 ft) long.

quality.notes: Kids need to know "silkworm", which makes 2 a bit low. Hint 2 ("a caterpillar") almost answers it. The silk photo could be illustrative rather than essential, but it works either way.

review.feedback: Hint 2 (“It's a caterpillar that eats mulberry leaves”) gives the answer away: the silkworm is the only caterpillar among the options, so hint 2 solves the question. It should be a vaguer clue, for example that the animal is much smaller than the other options, without naming caterpillars or mulberry. Also, no candidate shows shiny silk cloth. #2 is matte market fabric, #1 is a tissue ad, #3 and #4 are sketches, and #5 and #6 are Rolls-Royce cars. A new search is needed. No suitable picture found for this question.

previous.feedback: None of the media candidates shows clear, shiny silk cloth. 1–2 are samurai armour details, 3–4 are a crocheted gold jacket and 5–6 are piña (pineapple-fiber) cloth, which is a different material. Another search isn't allowed, so the slot needs new media, for example "silk fabric rolls" or "colorful silk scarves". It could also become illustrative with a query like "silk road caravan". No suitable picture found for this question.

revision.reason: No candidate showed silk cloth, so the media query is now a more concrete search for silk fabric.

media.note: A clear photo of shiny silk cloth or rolls of silk fabric, with no animals or cocoons visible.

questions.description: Every villain needs a favorite magic object, and this queen is very attached to hers.
questions.question: Jack is to the magic beans as the Evil Queen in “Snow White” is to the…
hints: It's the queen's own magical object.
She asks it who is the fairest of them all.
It hangs on the wall, and she looks into it.

media.credit: DimiTalen · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: DimiTalen

questions.fun_fact: In Disney's film the queen says “Magic mirror on the wall,” not “Mirror, mirror on the wall” as most people remember.

quality.notes: The analogy is a bit loose: the beans are Jack's trade, not really his own object. Hint 2 ("fairest of them all") is strong for a second hint.

questions.description: The original fashion designer, and the clients never get a bill.
questions.question: Who turns Cinderella's old rags into a beautiful dress for the royal ball?
hints: She appears when Cinderella is crying.
In the Disney film, she sings “Bibbidi-Bobbidi-Boo”.
She's a kind fairy who looks after Cinderella.

media.credit: Alicia Nijdam · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alicia Nijdam

questions.fun_fact: In the Brothers Grimm version, there's no fairy godmother: a magic tree and helpful birds give Cinderella her dress.

quality.notes: The description's "one wave" leans towards magic but doesn't settle it. The Grimm fun fact is accurate.

revision.reason: Rewrote the description so it no longer hints at a magic wand, and avoided "her" so the prince isn't ruled out.

previous.description: The original fashion designer: one wave and you're ready for the party.

questions.description: Its name is basically its old work schedule, which is a lot less catchy than “Nine-to-Five”.
questions.question: 7-Eleven is named after its first opening hours, 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. What kind of business is it?
questions.answer: A chain of small food stores
hints: The numbers 7 and 11 are times on the clock.
You might stop there for a quick snack on the way home.
Think of a little shop on the corner that sells snacks, drinks and milk.

media.credit: Paulo Barcellos Jr. · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Paulo Barcellos Jr.

questions.fun_fact: 7-Eleven started in Texas, but today the country with the most 7-Eleven stores is Japan.

quality.notes: This is brand knowledge that doesn't travel well: 7-Eleven is common in Asia and the US but almost unknown in much of Europe and Latin America. That leaves reasoning from the opening hours, which is weak. "Small food stores" undersells convenience stores slightly. The "Nine-to-Five" joke in the description is US-centric.

questions.description: A whole toolbox that went on a very strict diet.
questions.question: Which of these jobs could you do with this pocket knife?
hints: Look closely at the tools that fold out of it.
One of them is a small sharp blade.
Think about what a blade is best at.

media.note: A clear photo of a red Swiss Army knife with its blade and several tools folded out.
media.credit: Jonas Bergsten · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jonas Bergsten

questions.fun_fact: The first Swiss Army knife was made in 1891 for Swiss soldiers, so they could open cans of food and take apart their rifles.

quality.notes: Very trivial; you could answer it without the photo, since only one option is something a small folding knife does. That makes it feel like a test, not trivia, and it barely ties to the 'famous companies' theme. The wrong answers are silly rather than tempting. A photo of an open Swiss Army knife is easy to find, so the essential image is fine.

questions.description: A vegetable with more outfits than most people have in their closet.
questions.question: You're putting together Mr. Potato Head from “Toy Story”. Which of these is NOT a part you stick on him?
hints: Think about the parts of a face and a body.
Picture him grumbling on Andy's bed after his parts fall off.
The odd one out belongs on a car.

media.credit: Joenomias Menno De Jong · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joenomias Menno De Jong

questions.fun_fact: The first Mr. Potato Head, from 1952, came without a body: kids pushed the eyes, nose and mouth into a real potato!

quality.notes: Solid kids' question. The fun fact about the real potato is a nice touch.

questions.description: The architect's favorite way to put a lid on a really big building.
questions.question: Look at the top of this famous cathedral. What is this kind of roof called?
hints: Many churches, mosques and parliament buildings have one on top.
From inside, it looks like a giant bowl turned upside down.
An igloo has this shape too.

media.note: Close-up of the red-brick dome of Florence Cathedral, with only the dome filling the picture.
media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.fun_fact: The dome of the Pantheon in Rome is almost 2,000 years old and is still the largest dome made of unreinforced concrete in the world.

quality.notes: Young kids may not know 'gable' or 'turret', so the familiar word 'dome' stands out. It is a plain vocabulary question. The essential image and topic (Florence Cathedral dome) are the same as architectural-styles-14, but that question asks about a different fact.

questions.description: Ancient Rome's stadium floor crew had one very messy job.
questions.question: It covered the wooden floor of Rome's Colosseum, workers raked it smooth between shows, and it soaked up spills. What was it?
hints: It isn't something that grows.
It is made of tiny grains.
Every beach has lots of it.

media.credit: Charlottev96 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Charlottev96

questions.fun_fact: The word “arena” comes from the Latin word for sand.

quality.notes: Hint 1 removes two options at once, which is fine for a hint. The Latin 'arena' fun fact pays off nicely.

questions.description: A book where the rules painted on the wall keep changing overnight.
questions.question: In the novel where “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others”, which of these animals is NOT a character?
hints: The novel is George Orwell's “Animal Farm”.
Characters include Napoleon, Boxer and Moses, who tells tales of a land called Sugarcandy Mountain.
Other characters include a grumpy donkey, a goat, dogs, sheep and hens.

media.credit: Rodhullandemu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rodhullandemu

questions.fun_fact: Several publishers rejected “Animal Farm” before it finally came out in 1945, among them T. S. Eliot at Faber and Faber.
questions.concept: Todos los animales son iguales, pero algunos son más iguales que otros

quality.notes: You can reason it out because 'wolf' isn't a farm animal, but the raven keeps that guess from being too easy. Hint 1 names the book, which is acceptable.

questions.description: A motto that took a whole continent's worth of meetings to agree on.
questions.question: Which of these countries is NOT part of the union of countries whose motto is “United in diversity”?
hints: The union's flag shows a circle of twelve gold stars on blue.

media.credit: Max Braun · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Max Braun

questions.fun_fact: Norwegians voted against joining the European Union twice, in 1972 and in 1994.

quality.notes: Rated too hard. Players who think of the EU can pick out Norway easily, so most adults could answer: about 11, not 13. The question is fairly dry. Its lens is listed as 'popular_science', which doesn't fit.

questions.description: Family reunions in space are complicated.
questions.question: I'm a villain in purple armor, and in “Toy Story 2” I tell a space ranger toy that I am his father. Who am I?
hints: I'm a toy too.
My enemy says “To infinity and beyond!”
My name starts with the letter Z.

media.author: Tomascastelazo

questions.fun_fact: In the 2022 film “Lightyear,” Zurg turns out to be an older version of Buzz himself.

quality.notes: Darth Vader is a clever distractor and is clearly wrong because the question names Toy Story 2. The 'starts with Z' hint is strong but allowed as hint 3.

questions.description: Batman's worst enemy has a name that is no laughing matter.
questions.question: Where does the Joker, Batman's famous enemy, get his name from?
hints: You might find it in a game.
It often comes in pairs, and many games leave it out.
It's the wild card in the deck.

media.credit: Paulo Barcellos Jr. · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Paulo Barcellos Jr.

questions.fun_fact: The Joker first appeared in Batman #1 in 1940.

quality.notes: The playing-card origin is widely reported, but the creators' accounts differ a little. Players can tell which options are filler: a party hat and a circus tent aren't 'jokers'. The opening description of his looks doesn't help answer the question and makes it longer.

revision.reason: Cut the unhelpful opening sentence from the question, and replaced hint 2, which was wrong and too revealing, with a vaguer hint.

previous.question: He has green hair, white skin and a huge red grin, and he loves cruel pranks. Where does the Joker's name come from?
hints: You might find it in a game.
There are usually 52 others in the same box.
It's the wild card in the deck.

questions.description: A fish that could charge your phone, if it were in a better mood.
questions.question: This fish lives in South American rivers and can give strong electric shocks. What does it mostly use them for?
hints: Think about what every animal needs every day.
It has poor eyesight and lives in muddy water where it's hard to see.
It zaps its dinner.

media.note: A clear photo of an electric eel (Electrophorus) swimming.
media.credit: Steven G. Johnson · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Steven G. Johnson

questions.fun_fact: Despite its name, the electric eel is not a real eel at all: it is a kind of knifefish, related to catfish and carp.

quality.notes: Mostly correct. Electric eels also use their strong shocks for defense, and weak pulses for finding their way, but 'mostly … catching food' is defensible. 'Talking to birds' is a joke option, so there are really only two plausible distractors. Hint 2 practically gives the answer away.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which described stunned prey, with a medium-strength hint about poor eyesight in muddy water.

hints: Think about what every animal needs every day.
Small fish nearby suddenly can't move.
It zaps its dinner.

questions.description: A smile you would not want to see at the dentist.
questions.question: Look at this river fish's teeth. What are they best for?
hints: Look at how pointy they are.
They work a bit like scissors.
They snip off chunks of meat and fish.

media.note: A clear close-up photo of a piranha's open mouth showing its sharp triangular teeth.
media.credit: André-Philippe D. P. · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: André-Philippe D. P.

questions.fun_fact: Piranhas lose and regrow their teeth in groups, so they always have a sharp set ready.

quality.notes: The distractors are absurd ('Combing its fins', 'Chewing grass on land'), so the answer stands out even without the photo. As a question it is fairly flat. The essential piranha teeth photo is very likely available.

questions.description: No matter how fast the river runs, this part never leaves.
questions.question: It's the ground under a river's water. It can be sandy, muddy or rocky, and when a river dries up, you can walk along it. What is it?
hints: It's always underneath.
In clear water, you can see it from a boat.

questions.fun_fact: The Grand Canyon formed as the Colorado River cut its bed deeper and deeper over millions of years.

questions.description: Every great journey begins somewhere, even a very wet one.
questions.question: Every river starts its trip with me. I'm often a tiny spring or melting snow high up in the mountains. What am I?
hints: Look upstream, as far as you can go.

media.author: Faheem Ijaz Ch.

questions.fun_fact: The Amazon's farthest source is a small mountain stream high in the Andes of Peru.

questions.description: Who needs stars when you can rent the whole sky for one evening?
questions.question: Hundreds of lights rise into the night sky, draw a giant picture together for minutes, then fly back down and land. What makes these lights?
hints: They are machines, not animals.

media.author: Wilfredor

questions.fun_fact: In a drone light show, no person steers each drone: a computer program flies them all at the same time.

quality.notes: Drone light shows are newer and less familiar to 6-year-olds than the rating suggests, so 3–4 fits better. The clue "fly back down and land" cleanly rules out the other three options. An illustrative night-sky image would also have been safe. The q-5734 male bee "drone" shares only the word, not the fact.

questions.description: Small, shiny, and hiding inside more of your toys than you'd think.
questions.question: This little part hides inside toy cars, fans and robots. What does it do?
hints: It needs electricity to work.
In a robot, it lets the wheels and arms work.
Without it, a fan's blades would never go round.

media.note: A clear photo of a small electric motor (the kind found in toys), with its shaft visible and no label naming it.
media.credit: Evan-Amos · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Evan-Amos

questions.fun_fact: Electric motors use magnets to turn electricity into movement.

quality.notes: A reasonable but dry function question. Kids may not recognise a bare DC motor from a photo, but the hints help. Commons very likely has a clear photo of a small DC motor. It is related to q-2954 (motors make controllers vibrate) and q-4822 (a motor is not a sensor), but they ask different facts.

questions.description: Some robots copied the human body plan; others went their own way.
questions.question: You're sorting robots into ones built like a person, with a head, two arms and two legs. Which of these does NOT fit?
hints: Look at how each robot gets around.
The odd one out rolls instead of walking.
It rolls on tank tracks while it cleans up a lonely Earth.

media.credit: Vanillase · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vanillase

questions.fun_fact: Honda's humanoid robot ASIMO could walk, climb stairs and even run.

quality.notes: Optimus Prime counts as humanoid only in robot form, which is a small quibble. Kids may not know C-3PO or Optimus, but WALL·E alone is enough to get it. Hint 3 nearly names WALL·E, which is allowed. The description is more an explanation than a joke. It shares a topic with q-0177 (WALL·E compacting trash) but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Finally, a garden helper who never asks for a lunch break.
questions.question: You look over a garden fence and see a small robot rolling across the lawn all by itself. What is it doing?
hints: Its job keeps the lawn neat.
It has sharp spinning blades underneath.
People usually push a noisy machine around to do this job.

media.credit: Michael Garlick · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Garlick

questions.fun_fact: Many robot lawnmowers cut just a tiny bit every day and leave the clippings behind to feed the lawn.

quality.notes: "Painting the fence" is a throwaway distractor. Robot lawnmowers are common in some countries but rare in others, so the question travels less well. A "green garden lawn" search might return a photo with a mower in it, which is a slight risk.

questions.description: It works long shifts and never once complains about its feet.
questions.question: What job is this robot doing?
hints: It works where people go to eat.
It carries trays on its shelves.
It brings your order to your table.

media.note: A photo of a service robot in a restaurant carrying plates or trays of food, ideally next to tables.
media.credit: N509FZ · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: N509FZ

questions.fun_fact: Some restaurant robots show a cartoon cat face on their screen and react when you touch their heads.

quality.notes: The essential photo makes the answer obvious, which is fine at level 1. Openverse or Commons very likely has a restaurant robot photo, though a sharp one with food on board is less certain. The cat-face fun fact (Pudu BellaBot) is correct.

questions.description: Robots can do the robot dance, and so can you, thanks to this question's answer.
questions.question: Your elbow has one, a robot arm has several, and without them neither could bend. What is this part called?
hints: Your knees and fingers have them too.
On a robot, a small motor often sits inside it to turn it.
When your knee hurts, a doctor checks this part of it.

media.credit: Auledas · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Auledas

questions.fun_fact: Many factory robot arms have six joints, which lets them reach almost any angle, a bit like a human arm.

quality.notes: "Grandparents creak here" in the description points a little towards joints. The word "joint" may be a stretch for 6–9-year-olds. Hint 3 is weak, since a doctor checks more than the joint. The question is solid but rather school-like.

revision.reason: Rewrote the description so it no longer hints at creaky body joints.

previous.description: Robots and grandparents both creak here now and then.

questions.description: A glass pyramid where guitars go to retire in style.

hints: The city lies in the US Midwest.

It is in the state of Ohio.

questions.description: The man who heard a truck driver sing and thought: “That one.”

media.author: Rhododendrites

questions.description: An Irish band, an American desert and one very spiky plant.
questions.question: In which year did U2 release “The Joshua Tree”, the album with “With or Without You”?
hints: It came out in the second half of a decade.

media.author: Tuxyso

hints: It came out in the second half of a decade.

hints: The amphitheater lies in a town buried by a volcano in the year 79.
The band was from London and known for long, spacey songs and huge light shows.
The band later made the album “The Dark Side of the Moon”.

media.author: Commonists

revision.reason: Hint 2 no longer names the album, and hint 3 replaces the color clue, which also fit Deep Purple, with the album clue.

hints: The amphitheater lies in a town buried by a volcano in the year 79.
The band later made the album “The Dark Side of the Moon”.
The band's name includes a color.

questions.description: Roman grown-ups had a favorite drink, and it was not a milkshake.
questions.question: Romans made it from crushed grapes, mixed it with water before drinking, and Bacchus was its god. What drink was it?
hints: It is a drink for grown-ups, not for kids.
Its color can be red or white.
Vineyards grow the fruit for it.

media.author: Fabio Ingrosso

questions.fun_fact: Drinking wine without water was seen as bad manners in ancient Rome.

questions.description: Some emperors collect statues; this one collected walls.
questions.question: I'm the Roman emperor who moved the frontier in Britain north of my predecessor's wall and built a turf wall from the Forth to the Clyde. Who am I?
hints: I ruled right after the emperor whose wall in Britain is most famous.
My reign was known as unusually peaceful.
My turf wall in Scotland is named after me, just as the more famous wall is named after my predecessor.

media.author: Peer Lawther from Leeds, United Kingdom

questions.description: A royal project with marble, famous sculptors and absolutely no budget limit.
questions.question: Around 350 BC, Queen Artemisia II of Caria finished a giant marble building decorated by top Greek sculptors. It became one of the Seven Wonders. What was it for?
hints: It stood in Halicarnassus, today the town of Bodrum in Turkey.
Its name gave us a word still used for grand buildings of this kind.
Her husband was King Mausolus.

media.credit: Serhio Magpie · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Serhio Magpie

questions.fun_fact: Knights later took stones from the ruined Mausoleum to build Bodrum Castle, which still stands by the harbor.

quality.notes: Saying Artemisia 'finished' the building is a stretch: ancient sources say work went on after she died around 351 BC. The Mausoleum is fairly well known, and the 'Artemisia/Artemis' trap is clever, so 14 is a bit high. Hint 2 points strongly to 'mausoleum', which is acceptable for a hint.

review.feedback: This overlaps the approved q-3138 (“The Taj Mahal is to Mumtaz Mahal as the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus is to… Mausolus”). Both questions rest on the same fact: the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was the tomb of King Mausolus. q-3138 tells players the building is a tomb, and this question's hint 3 names Mausolus, so each one gives the other away. Separately, saying Artemisia “finished” the building is doubtful, because ancient sources say work went on after she died around 351 BC.

questions.description: Just you, the ball, a nervous goalkeeper and a few million people holding their breath.

questions.description: A coin that couldn't pick an outfit, so it wore two.

questions.description: Indian music has rules too, and some of them are even older than your grandma's recipes.

questions.description: Two strings, one bow, and a sound that can make a stone cry.

quality.notes: The erhu is fairly well known, so 15 is a little high. By sound alone, an erhu is hard to tell from a morin khuur, so the clue in the name carries the question. A solo erhu recording on Freesound or Commons is likely. The media has no background_query, which audio questions need.

review.feedback: Neither audio candidate is an erhu: both are Indian dance performances recorded at Khajuraho, and a new search isn't possible. The essential audio slot needs a real solo erhu recording, for example from a search for "erhu solo" on Freesound or Commons. If none can be found, the question can't be played as a "Listen:" question. No suitable picture found for this question.

review.feedback: The question says Colombia's Mother's Day is the last Sunday of May. Nationally it is the second Sunday of May (Ley 28 de 1925); only Cúcuta celebrates it on the last Sunday. Change the question text to "segundo domingo de mayo". The rater note also confirms the second Sunday. Verificación de datos: wrong. In Colombia, Mother's Day is the second Sunday of May (Law 28 of 1925). Only Cúcuta moves it to the last Sunday of May.

previous.feedback: The date is wrong: Colombia celebrates Mother's Day on the last Sunday of May (law from 1925), not the second Sunday like the USA and Mexico's neighbours. The rater's note confirming the second Sunday is mistaken.

revision.reason: Corrected the date: Colombia celebrates Mother's Day on the last Sunday of May.

questions.description: Un departamento donde hasta el «buenos días» suena con carácter.

hints: Se le dice a mamá, a la profe y a los mayores.
Viene del verbo «mandar».
Es como decir «estoy a sus órdenes».

media.credit: Luis Eduardo White Patiño · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luis Eduardo White Patiño

questions.fun_fact: «Mande» viene de «mandar»: es como decir «mándeme, que estoy para servirle».

quality.notes: '¿Qué necesita?' is a fair gloss of '¿mande?'. 'Ya voy para allá' is arguably close in use. The fun fact repeats hint 2 ('viene de mandar'). The question is somewhat flat.

questions.description: Las palabras colombianas tienen más estados de ánimo que un lunes festivo.
questions.question: ¿Cuál de estas expresiones colombianas NO sirve para decir que algo es bueno o divertido?
hints: Tres de ellas las dirías en una fiesta buenísima.
La otra la dirías en una clase que no se acaba nunca.
En Colombia se dice cuando algo es aburridísimo o fastidioso.

media.credit: Andres Franco · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andres Franco

questions.fun_fact: «Jartera» viene de «jartarse», la forma popular de «hartarse»: estar lleno o cansado de algo.

quality.notes: Clean. Hint 2 already nearly gives the answer away.

questions.description: Ni tan chiquito para la piñata, ni tan grande para el tinto.
questions.question: En Bogotá le dicen así a quien ya no es niño pero tampoco adulto: anda en bachillerato y se enamora a cada rato. ¿Qué palabra es?
hints: Tiene más o menos entre 12 y 17 años.
Los adultos lo dicen medio con cariño, medio en burla, de los que empiezan a ir a fiestas y a tener novio o novia.
Su versión femenina viene en lata.

media.credit: Felipe Restrpo Acosta · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Felipe Restrpo Acosta

questions.fun_fact: Los rolos también dicen «chino» o «china» para hablar de un niño o un muchacho.

quality.notes: 'Sardino' is used across Colombia, not only in Bogotá, but that's fine. Good slang distractors. Hint 3 is a fun clue.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which pointed to the sea, with a hint about how adults use the word.

hints: Tiene más o menos entre 12 y 17 años.

questions.description: Aquí vive tanta gente que hasta el tinto tiene que hacer fila.
questions.question: Es la región donde vive la mayoría de los colombianos, la cruzan tres cordilleras y en ella está Bogotá. ¿Cuál es?
hints: Es la región de las montañas.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.fun_fact: En Colombia la cordillera de los Andes se divide en tres ramales: Occidental, Central y Oriental.

quality.notes: Correct and clear. Mentioning Bogotá makes it trivial for Colombian kids, which is fine at this level, though a 6-year-old may not know the region names yet, so 3 fits better than 2. Plain school-geography fact, and the 'history' lens doesn't fit. Shares a topic with q-0552 (region Andina), but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Cuatro huecos, una caña y un soplido: el Carnaval no necesita más.
questions.question: La flauta de millo se toca de lado y su lengüeta se corta en la misma caña. ¿Qué es el millo?
hints: La flauta se fabrica con la caña de lo que le da su nombre.
En la Costa Caribe también se siembra por sus semillas o para alimentar animales.
Su caña es delgada y hueca, como la de su pariente el mijo.

media.credit: Camilo1982 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Camilo1982

questions.fun_fact: La flauta de millo también se llama caña de millo o pito atravesao, y es la reina del Carnaval de Barranquilla.

quality.notes: The question's three facts describe the flute, not the plant, so they don't help answer what 'millo' is. It's an odd setup. The correct answer is the longest and most specific option ('parecida al sorgo') and stands out. Few Colombians know the botany, so it's harder than 9. Hint 3 (mijo) nearly gives it away, which is allowed for hint 3.

review.feedback: The fact check is 'uncertain', and I can't confirm from my own knowledge which plant 'millo' is. Sources disagree: some describe a grass like corn, others sorghum or millet. That makes the answer 'Una planta parecida al sorgo' and hint 3's 'su pariente el mijo' unconfirmable. Also, the question's clues only describe the flute, not the plant, so they don't help players work out the answer. The correct option is longer and more specific than the wrong ones and stands out. Verificación de datos: uncertain. In Colombia 'millo' is often described as a plant similar to corn (maíz) or as sorghum/millet. 'Parecida al sorgo' and the hint about 'su pariente el mijo' are shaky and could not be verified.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which said the plant is a cereal grass, with a vaguer hint about how it is grown, and shortened the question.

questions.description: En Neiva, en junio, hasta el calor se pone sombrero.

questions.description: En Córdoba, cuando dicen que va a sonar una banda, no se refieren a una de rock.
questions.question: En el Festival Nacional del Porro de San Pelayo, Córdoba, compiten bandas sabaneras. ¿Qué instrumentos las forman?
wrong_answers: Gaitas, maracas, tambor alegre y llamador
hints: Son las mismas bandas que animan corralejas y fiestas de pueblo.

quality.notes: Accurate: the bandas pelayeras/papayeras line-up is right. The distractors are good, matching Colombian ensembles. The answer is a list of instruments, which makes it a little dry, and the 'body_senses' lens is a stretch.

questions.description: Una canción que lleva más de medio siglo navegando por el río sin hundirse.
questions.question: Una cumbia famosísima cuenta la historia de una embarcación como esta: la de Guillermo Cubillos. ¿Quién la compuso?
hints: Era de El Banco, Magdalena.

questions.description: La fruta que prefiere terminar en salsa picante antes que en postre.
questions.question: Soy ovalado y ácido, de cáscara roja o anaranjada. Me licúan para jugo y me muelen con ají para las empanadas. ¿Qué soy?

hints: El dicho compara a una persona con el lugar que tiene el arroz en la mesa colombiana.

media.author: Douglas Perkins

Hint 2 shouldn't name the tuber base. The "suero" pairing in hint 2 is also shaky (it is usually served with white rice) and should be dropped.

'De teclado' is a weak distractor. It's a fairly dry family-classification question. q-4063 also has percussion as its answer but asks about orchestra families, so the overlap is only mild.

review.feedback: Hint 1 ("No tiene teclas ni cuerdas, y tampoco se sopla") rules out all three wrong answers, so it gives the answer away. Replace it with a vague hint, for example one about the guacharaca's role in the vallenato trio or about what it is made of (cane or wood), that doesn't eliminate any option.

The question ("Este instrumento…") only works with an essential photo of the instrument. Either find a real photo of a guacharaca with its trinche, or rework the question to name the instrument in the text and use an illustrative image (for example a vallenato ensemble or a caja vallenata). hints: Ya pasaron la Navidad y los Reyes.
Cae a comienzos del segundo mes del año.
Es exactamente 40 días después de la Navidad.

questions.concept: Fiesta de la Candelaria de Cartagena

quality.notes: Correct. Candlemas on 2 February is fairly common knowledge among Catholic Colombian adults, so 12 is a bit high. The description's 'velas' nudges towards Candelaria. It's a fairly dry date question.

questions.description: En Cali hasta los semáforos se mueven al ritmo de la clave.
questions.question: En la Feria de Cali todo el mundo sale a bailar salsa. ¿Cuál de estas cosas NO es un baile?
hints: Tres de ellas suenan en las fiestas de Colombia.
Una de ellas no la puedes escuchar en un parlante.

questions.fun_fact: A Cali le dicen la capital mundial de la salsa, y en su feria hay un desfile llamado Salsódromo.

revision.reason: Rewrote hints 1 and 2 so they build up indirectly instead of saying the answer is food.

hints: Tres de ellas se bailan con música.
Una se come en el desayuno.
Es redonda, de maíz y se le pone queso.

questions.description: Un día en que nadie en Pasto sale a la calle con la cara limpia.
questions.question: El 5 de enero en Pasto te pintan la cara de negro. Según la tradición, ¿quiénes pidieron ese día libre en la época colonial?
hints: Fue en el siglo XVII.
No tenían ningún día de descanso.
Los trajeron a la fuerza desde África.

media.author: Hanksol

questions.fun_fact: Según la tradición, la Corona española concedió ese día libre después de una revuelta en 1607.

quality.notes: It's presented as tradition (the 1607 revolt and a day off granted), which is accurate. 'Los estudiantes del colegio' is an absurd distractor for the colonial era, and the face-painting clue makes the answer easy to reason out. It touches on slavery but stays neutral, which is acceptable.

questions.description: En el desfile de Barranquilla, el Torito persigue a la gente y todos salen corriendo muertos de risa.
questions.question: El Zorro la usa, el Torito del Carnaval de Barranquilla la lleva con cachos y te tapa la cara. ¿Cómo se llama?
hints: En Barranquilla muchas se tallan a mano en madera.
También las hay de animales, como el tigre, el burro o la Marimonda.
También le dicen máscara.

media.credit: Ryan Hodnett · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ryan Hodnett

questions.fun_fact: Las caretas de animales del Carnaval de Barranquilla se tallan a mano en pueblos como Galapa.

quality.notes: El Zorro also wears a capa, and his mask is a tied cloth that could pass for a pañoleta; only the Torito clue settles it. Hint 3 ('máscara') basically states the answer. This is close to q-5041 (Barranquilla masks), but that one asks for the city.

revision.reason: New description without the hiding-your-face idea, and hints 1 and 2 replaced: one was wrong, the other gave the answer away.

previous.description: Para ir de incógnito al carnaval sin que tu tía te reconozca.
hints: No va en la cabeza ni en la espalda.
Tiene huecos para los ojos.
También le dicen máscara.

questions.description: Una guerra en la que todos pierden y todos salen felices.
questions.question: En el Carnaval de Barranquilla la gente juega a tirarse cosas. ¿Cuál de estas NO se tiran jugando?
hints: Tres de ellas no dejan la ropa pegajosa.
La que sobra se unta en el pan.
Es dulce y se hace con fruta.

questions.fun_fact: En el carnaval mucha gente sale con gafas para protegerse los ojos de la espuma y la maicena.

quality.notes: The question text names 'espuma', which is also one of the wrong options, so it gives one away. For a difficulty-1 question that's fine.

revision.reason: Replaced 'Maicena' with 'Confeti' to avoid overlap with q-7095, removed 'espuma' from the question text and adapted hint 1.

hints: Tres de ellas se lavan fácil.
La que sobra se unta en el pan.
Es dulce y se hace con fruta.

questions.description: Un cineasta que prefería a los muchachos del barrio antes que a las estrellas de Hollywood.
questions.question: Dirigí 'Rodrigo D. No futuro' y 'La vendedora de rosas', las dos en competencia en Cannes, con actores naturales de Medellín. ¿Quién soy?
hints: Soy de Antioquia y también soy poeta.
Mis películas muestran la vida de jóvenes de las comunas de Medellín.

media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.fun_fact: Para 'La vendedora de rosas' (1998), Gaviria trabajó con niños y jóvenes que vivían en las calles de Medellín, en vez de actores profesionales.

quality.notes: Facts check out. One small doubt: 'Sumas y restas' showed at festivals in 2004 but only came out in Colombia in 2005, so 'estrené en 2004' is slightly loose. The description hints at amateur actors from the neighbourhood, which overlaps with the clue in the question. The question is a fairly dry list of a filmography.

revision.reason: Removed 'antioqueño' from the description so it no longer points to the director's region.

previous.description: Un antioqueño que prefería a los muchachos del barrio antes que a las estrellas de Hollywood.

questions.description: Unos inmigrantes que trajeron de Italia algo más útil que una receta de pasta.
questions.question: Llegamos de Italia, abrimos el Salón Olympia en Bogotá y en 1915 filmamos 'El drama del 15 de octubre'. ¿Quiénes somos?
hints: Somos pioneros del cine en Colombia, de comienzos del siglo XX.
Nuestro salón de cine en Bogotá abrió sus puertas en 1912.
Nuestro apellido suena a 'domingo' en italiano.

media.credit: Pathé Frères (progettista/ costruttore) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pathé Frères (progettista/ costruttore)

questions.fun_fact: 'El drama del 15 de octubre' contaba un hecho político real de Bogotá y causó tanta polémica que la película se perdió casi por completo.

quality.notes: Hermanos Acevedo is a strong distractor. Lumière and Taviani are easy to rule out (Lumière were French, not immigrants who came from Italy). Hint 3 (Domenico ≈ domingo) almost gives the answer away, which is allowed for hint 3. The fun fact about polemics leading to the film's loss is somewhat simplified.

questions.description: La alcancía oficial de los cineastas colombianos.
questions.question: ¿En qué década se creó Proimágenes Colombia, el fondo mixto que hoy administra el Fondo para el Desarrollo Cinematográfico?
hints: Nació poco después de que se cerrara Focine.
Surgió gracias a la Ley General de Cultura.

media.author: Bernd Schwabe in Hannover

questions.fun_fact: Proimágenes nació en 1998, y desde la Ley de Cine de 2003 administra el dinero que se recauda de la taquilla para hacer nuevas películas.

quality.notes: Correct (founded 1998, after the 1997 Ley General de Cultura). Very dry institutional question: a decade for a funding body. Related to q-5035 (Focine) but asks a different fact. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is fine.

questions.description: Un sueño americano que empieza haciendo fila en una embajada.
questions.question: ¿En qué década se estrenó 'Visa USA', la película de Lisandro Duque sobre un joven que sueña con irse a Estados Unidos?
hints: Se hizo en la época de Focine.
Por esos años también se estrenó 'Tras la esmeralda perdida', con Michael Douglas.
Salió el mismo año del Mundial de México con Maradona.

media.credit: Jon Evans · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jon Evans

questions.fun_fact: 'Visa USA' (1986) es una de las películas colombianas más recordadas de la época de Focine.

quality.notes: Visa USA (1986) is correct, and the hints check out (Romancing the Stone 1984, Mexico 1986). A dry decade question about a film.

questions.description: Una niña que se salió de su libro sin pedirle permiso al autor.
questions.question: ¿En qué década se estrenó 'El libro de Lila', la película animada de Marcela Rincón hecha en Cali?
hints: Es una película bastante reciente.
Cuenta la historia de una niña que se cae de su libro a un mundo de papel.

questions.fun_fact: 'El libro de Lila' (2017) fue uno de los primeros largometrajes animados hechos en Colombia que llegaron a las salas de cine.

quality.notes: Correct (2017). A recent Colombian animated feature is easy to guess as the 2010s, and the 1980s option is barely plausible. Hint 2 (Encanto) almost settles it. 'One of the first' animated features in cinemas is vague. Dry decade question.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which pinned the decade via Encanto, with a hint about the film's story.

hints: Es una película bastante reciente.
Se estrenó pocos años antes que 'Encanto'.
Salió unos años después del Mundial de Brasil, donde brilló James Rodríguez.

questions.description: Un cartagenero que decidió que la ciudad amurallada también necesitaba pantallas.
questions.question: ¿En qué década fundó Víctor Nieto el Festival Internacional de Cine de Cartagena de Indias?
hints: Se considera el festival de cine más antiguo de Latinoamérica.
Sus premios se llaman India Catalina.
Nació poco después de la Revolución cubana.

media.author: Igvir Ramirez

questions.fun_fact: El festival nació en 1960, y Víctor Nieto lo dirigió durante más de 40 años.

quality.notes: Founded 1960 is correct. 'Oldest festival in Latin America' is the usual claim but is disputed. A dry decade question. A well-read Colombian adult can reason it out with the hints, so 13–14 rather than 15.

questions.description: Un equipo de Manizales que se fue de paseo por Sudamérica y volvió con la copa en la maleta.
questions.question: Para ganar la Copa Libertadores 2004, el Once Caldas eliminó a tres de estos gigantes. ¿A cuál NO enfrentó?
hints: Fíjate en los equipos brasileños: en ese torneo el Once se cruzó con dos de ellos.
La final se jugó contra un equipo argentino y se definió por penales.

media.author: Erik Albers

questions.fun_fact: En la final de 2004, el arquero Juan Carlos Henao fue figura en la tanda de penales que le dio la Copa al Once Caldas contra Boca Juniors.

quality.notes: Facts check out: Barcelona SC, then Santos, São Paulo and Boca (in the final, on penalties). Calling Boca 'eliminated' in a final is a slight stretch but understandable. Recalling which teams they played in the knockout rounds is fan-level knowledge, so maybe 11.

questions.description: Una cancha donde el calor del San Pedro se siente hasta en los camerinos.
questions.question: «Estoy en Neiva, a orillas del río Magdalena, y en mi grama juega de local el Atlético Huila». ¿Cómo me llamo?
hints: Los cuatro son nombres de estadios colombianos que homenajean a una persona.
Mi nombre homenajea a un dirigente político del propio Huila.

questions.fun_fact: El equipo femenino del Atlético Huila fue campeón de la Copa Libertadores Femenina en 2018, el primer título continental para un club colombiano de mujeres.

quality.notes: Stadium names are dry trivia: it's really just 'what is Neiva's stadium called'. The distractors are good real stadiums. Hint 3 gives away the surname, which is allowed for hint 3.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which eliminated all three wrong answers, with a clue about the stadium's namesake.

hints: Los cuatro son nombres de estadios colombianos que homenajean a una persona.
Descarta los de Ibagué, Pereira y Cali.

questions.description: El momento en que toda Colombia deja de respirar frente al televisor.
questions.question: Cuando una final de la Liga colombiana termina empatada, se patean penales como este. ¿Cuántos cobra cada equipo antes de la muerte súbita?
hints: Son menos que los jugadores que hay en la cancha.
Es la mitad de diez.
Son tantos como los dedos de una mano.

questions.fun_fact: Si después de los cinco cobros sigue el empate, se patea uno por uno hasta que un equipo falle y el otro anote: eso es la muerte súbita.

quality.notes: The photo isn't really essential (the question doesn't depend on it); illustrative would fit better. '11' is a weak distractor. Hints 2 and 3 both give the number away in effect. Rather dry rule question.

review.feedback: This asks the same fact as approved q-2488: how many kicks each team takes at first in a penalty shootout (5). Putting it in the Colombian league doesn't change the fact. Separately, hint 2 ("la mitad de diez") already gives the number away.

questions.description: Ganar una vez es suerte, dos es costumbre, y tres seguidas ya es para mandar a hacer camisetas.
questions.question: Hasta 2025, ¿en cuál de estas ciudades nunca había habido un club tricampeón, con tres títulos seguidos de la liga colombiana?
hints: Piensa en las estrellas que los clubes llevan sobre el escudo y en sus grandes rachas.

media.author: Matt Boulton

questions.fun_fact: El América de Cali fue pentacampeón entre 1982 y 1986, y Millonarios tetracampeón entre 1961 y 1964.

quality.notes: Checked: Millonarios (1951–53, 1961–64), Nacional (2013–14), América (1982–86); Junior never won three in a row. Hint 1 points strongly to the three other cities. Fairly dry stats question.

revision.reason: Anchored the fact to 2025 and made hints 1 and 2 vaguer so they no longer eliminate the wrong cities.

previous.question: ¿En cuál de estas ciudades NUNCA ha habido un club tricampeón, con tres títulos seguidos de la liga colombiana?

El América llegó a ganar cinco seguidos en los años ochenta.
Es la ciudad del Junior, que tiene muchas estrellas, pero nunca tres en fila.

questions.description: Un ascensor que nadie quiere tomar hacia abajo.
questions.question: Si un equipo pierde la categoría en la Primera A del fútbol colombiano, ¿en qué torneo juega la siguiente temporada?

media.author: Nazmi Amin-Tai from Melaka, Malaysia

quality.notes: The distractors are weak: Copa Sudamericana and Superliga are obviously not where a relegated team plays, so Primera B is the only real candidate once you see 'Primera A' in the question. Easier than 6.

questions.description: Un club tan anaranjado que parece jugo de naranja con guayos.

questions.fun_fact: El apodo viene de la selección de Países Bajos de los años setenta, famosa por su camiseta naranja y su fútbol total.

questions.description: El orden de los factores sí altera el producto, al menos en el marcador.
questions.question: En la tele ves el marcador «Junior 0 - 1 Nacional». Por costumbre, el equipo que aparece primero es…

questions.fun_fact: Jugar de local es una ventaja real: en casi todas las ligas del mundo, los equipos ganan más partidos en su propio estadio.

questions.description: Un papelito de colores que pesa más que un balón.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which described the consequence, with a traffic-light colour hint.

hints: No es una buena noticia para el jugador.

questions.description: Telas tan largas que con una se podría tapar media tribuna.

hints: Es un país sudamericano.

questions.description: Sin ella, la cicla se queda en la casa con cara de domingo lluvioso.
questions.question: Se te desinfló la llanta de la cicla y te ofrecen «la bomba». ¿Qué te están ofreciendo?

previous.feedback: The fact check is 'uncertain' and I can't confirm it either: sources disagree on which aires the Bunde tolimense blends. Some say guabina, torbellino and bambuco. Spanish Wikipedia adds rajaleña, pasillo, vals, chotis and others. English Wikipedia names bambuco, vals, danza and pasillo. That means the distractors 'Pasillo, danza y vals' and 'Pasillo, chotis y bambuco' are partly defensible. Hint 3 also ties guabina to Boyacá and Santander, but it is just as much a Tolima/Huila rhythm. Either ask about a fact that isn't disputed (for example the composer or the song's status as the department's anthem), or replace the distractors with rhythms that no source links to the Bunde. Verificación de datos: uncertain. Sources disagree. Some give guabina, torbellino and bambuco. The Spanish Wikipedia lists rajaleña, pasillo, guabina, torbellino and bambuco, plus vals, mazurka, redova and chotis. The English Wikipedia lists bambuco, vals, danza and pasillo. So 'three aires' is ambiguous, and the distractors 'Pasillo, chotis y bambuco' and 'Pasillo, danza y vals' partly overlap with documented elements. Also, the Tolima anthem version has lyrics by Nicanor Velásquez, which the question doesn't mention.

revision.reason: Sources disagree on which rhythms the Bunde blends, so I now ask about its composer, which is undisputed, and gave it new distractors and hints.

review.feedback: The description says the river has "a Roman general's name". Players will take that to mean it was named after Julius Caesar. The name Cesar actually comes from an indigenous word (Zazare/Chet-tzar), not from Rome, so the description teaches a false origin. Replace it with a playful line that doesn't mention the name's origin, e.g. «Un río que nace en la nieve y termina en una ciénaga gigante.» Verificación de datos: wrong. The answer is right, but the description says the river is named after a Roman general. The name Cesar comes from a native cacique (Zazare/Upar), not from Rome.

previous.feedback: The question text says "Este es el río Cesar", so the picture has to show the Cesar River. Candidates 1 and 2 show the Guatapurí, a different river (a tributary at Valledupar). Candidate 3 is an unidentified rocky gorge with nothing to place it. No new search is allowed, so the slot needs a real photo of the Cesar River, e.g. from a search for "Cesar River Colombia". Another option is to drop "Este es" and use a decorative Cesar-region image. No se encontró una imagen adecuada para esta pregunta.

revision.reason: No photo of the Cesar River exists, so I dropped 'Este es' and switched the image to the Zapatosa swamp that the question names.

Separately, "Una zorra" works as a crude insult for a woman in Colombia and much of Latin America, so a family game shouldn't use it as an option. Distractors: Jan Bijvoet and Brionne Davis are the film's foreign lead actors, and their non-Spanish names rule them out for an Indigenous shaman. Hint 1 makes this explicit, which leaves a coin-flip between two Spanish names. Age fit and difficulty: the cast of an arthouse film is very niche even for Colombian adults, closer to a 15 than a 14. It is also pure recall with nothing to reason towards. Fun: it's a dry fact, with only a little charm from the Bolívar surname link in hint 3. The Amazon rainforest image is safe.

review.feedback: None of the candidates works as the essential map. Candidate 1 is a map of South America with 'Bogota' written on it, which gives the answer away. Candidates 2 and 3 highlight Amazonas and Antioquia, not Bogotá. A new search isn't allowed, so the slot needs a clean, unlabeled locator map of Colombia with Bogotá D.C. highlighted. previous.feedback: Hints 1 and 2 already give the answer away for Colombian players: 'the largest city in the country' and 'where the president works' each mean Bogotá immediately, just like hint 3. Hint 1 should be vague, for example about the stadium's location or the city's cool highland climate without saying it's the biggest, and hint 2 should be only moderately strong. Media candidate 1 is usable but weak: the Colombia inset with the red mark is small, and most of the picture is the shape of the district.

revision.reason: Made hints 1 and 2 vaguer so they don't give away Bogotá before hint 3; kept the usable map.

quality.notes: Facts check out: Pombo was born in Bogotá in 1833, the three poems are his, he lived in New York from about 1855 to 1872 and adapted children's tales there, and the Fundación Rafael Pombo exists. Popayán and Cartagena are smart wrong options because his family had roots in both. Fun: a 'where was he born' question is fairly dry, and since Bogotá is the default guess for any famous Colombian, many players will get it by guessing rather than by thinking it through. Hint 1 ('clima frío') already rules out Cartagena and Medellín, which is strong for a first hint. Description: the 'cédula' joke is mild and only loosely funny, though it doesn't give anything away. The decorative image is acceptable, since an illustrative image of Pombo's work could show his name. No overlap: the other Bogotá questions ask about different facts.
