questions.description: Una palabra que a veces pesa más que quien la carga.
questions.question: En Colombia, ¿qué es un morral?
questions.answer: Un bolso que se carga en la espalda
wrong_answers: Una caja para llevar el almuerzo
Un estuche para lápices y colores
hints: Lo usas para ir al colegio.
Casi siempre tiene cierre y viene de muchos colores.
Tiene dos correas para los hombros.

media.credit: Dobrislava · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dobrislava

questions.fun_fact: En Colombia la «mochila» suele ser la tejida a mano, como la wayuu o la arhuaca, y el bolso escolar es el morral.

quality.notes: A simple vocabulary question that is a bit dry. The heaviness joke in the description mildly points to a bag. The fun fact about the wayuu mochila is nice.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which ruled out every wrong option, with a vaguer clue about the zipper and the colours.

hints: Lo usas para ir al colegio.
Ahí van los cuadernos y la cartuchera.
Tiene dos correas para los hombros.

questions.description: Un istmo que en 1821 decidió que mejor era no vivir solo.
questions.question: Panamá se independizó de España el 28 de noviembre de 1821. ¿A qué país se unió poco después por voluntad propia?
wrong_answers: A las Provincias Unidas del Centro de América
hints: Fue un país que ya no existe con ese nombre.
Su nombre nació de un sueño de unir a varias naciones sudamericanas.
Incluía a la actual Colombia, Venezuela y Ecuador.

media.credit: Holacocacola1968 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Holacocacola1968

questions.fun_fact: Panamá se independizó de España casi sin combates: se cuenta que buena parte de las tropas españolas fue convencida con dinero para no pelear.

quality.notes: The bribery fun fact is commonly told and is hedged with 'se cuenta', which is acceptable.

questions.description: Un país tan grande que al final no cupo en sí mismo.
questions.question: Cuando la Gran Colombia se disolvió, hacia 1830, ¿en cuántos países quedó dividida?
hints: Panamá todavía no se había separado.
Uno de ellos se llamó República de la Nueva Granada.
Venezuela fue uno de ellos.

media.credit: Arturo Michelena · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arturo Michelena

questions.fun_fact: La bandera de Colombia, la de Venezuela y la de Ecuador comparten el amarillo, el azul y el rojo como recuerdo de la Gran Colombia.

quality.notes: A plain counting question, somewhat school-like.

questions.description: Un parque donde nadie iba a montar en columpio.
questions.question: Según la historia patria, en San Mateo en 1814 Antonio Ricaurte prefirió destruir el «parque» de Bolívar antes que entregarlo. ¿Qué era?
questions.answer: El depósito de pólvora y municiones
wrong_answers: La caja con el dinero de la tropa
hints: En el lenguaje militar de la época, «parque» no significaba lo mismo que hoy.
Ricaurte lo custodiaba en la casa alta de la hacienda mientras Bolívar combatía abajo.
Hoy se le diría también polvorín.

media.credit: Martin Tovar y Tovar · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Martin Tovar y Tovar

questions.fun_fact: Ricaurte nació en Villa de Leyva, y hoy un municipio de Cundinamarca y otro de Nariño llevan su nombre.

quality.notes: A fun twist on the word 'parque'. Portraits of Ricaurte often show the explosion, which slightly risks a giveaway. The answer is a little longer than the other options.

revision.reason: Replaced hints 1 and 2, which pointed straight at the gunpowder depot, with vaguer hints that don't mention explosions or shooting.

hints: Era algo que podía explotar.
Los realistas lo querían para seguir disparando.
Hoy se le diría también polvorín.

questions.description: Cuando el bastón de mando cambia de mano, cambia la historia.
questions.question: El 4 de julio de 1810, en Pamplona, una mujer enfrentó al corregidor español y le quitó el bastón de mando. ¿Quién fue?
hints: Era una criolla de Pamplona, de familia acomodada.
Su gesto fue antes del 20 de julio.
Su apellido de casada era Villamizar.

media.credit: EEIM · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: EEIM

questions.fun_fact: Bolívar llamó a Pamplona «Ciudad Patriótica» por haber sido pionera en el grito de independencia.

quality.notes: The facts about Águeda Gallardo are right. I'm not sure Bolívar personally gave Pamplona the title 'Ciudad Patriótica'. She is lesser-known regional history, possibly 12.

questions.description: Tres meses de caminata por las montañas, con botas y sin GPS.
questions.question: En 1813 Bolívar partió de la Nueva Granada, cruzó los Andes venezolanos y en unos tres meses entró triunfante a Caracas. ¿Cómo se llama esa campaña?
hints: No es la de 1819 que terminó en Boyacá.
Empezó cerca de Cúcuta.
Su nombre expresa asombro.

media.credit: José Luis Valero · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: José Luis Valero

questions.fun_fact: Bolívar empezó esta campaña con menos de mil soldados y aun así atravesó todo el occidente de Venezuela hasta Caracas.

quality.notes: The fun fact about the title 'El Libertador' repeats the fact asked in q-7518, though this question itself asks something different. It is a school-history question. Hint 3 ('expresa asombro') is strong.

revision.reason: Replaced the fun fact, which was inaccurate (Mérida gave the title first) and repeated q-7518, with one about the campaign's small army.

previous.fun_fact: Al final de esta campaña, en Caracas, Bolívar empezó a ser llamado públicamente «el Libertador».

questions.description: Una dama del monte con la que es mejor no salir a caminar.
questions.question: Me aparezco en el monte como una mujer bonita para engañar a cazadores y leñadores, pero ando a saltos larguísimos porque me falta algo. ¿Quién soy?
hints: Protejo la selva de quienes la dañan.
Lo que me falta está del cuerpo para abajo.
Tengo una sola pierna.

media.credit: Päivi & Santeri · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Päivi & Santeri

questions.fun_fact: Dicen que la Patasola puede dar saltos tan largos que alcanza a cualquiera que corra por la selva, ¡aunque tenga una sola pata!

quality.notes: The fun fact mostly repeats the clue. The Madremonte and the Tunda are good distractors.

questions.description: Un juego de gentilicios para ver quién se sabe el mapa de memoria.
questions.question: Completa: Medellín es a paisa como Bucaramanga es a…
hints: Es la capital de un departamento del nororiente colombiano.
Allá la gente tiene fama de hablar fuerte y de tratar de «usted» hasta a los hijos.
Es la tierra del cañón del Chicamocha y de las hormigas culonas.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.fun_fact: A muchos santandereanos les dicen «bravos» por su forma de hablar, aunque solo estén conversando tranquilos.

quality.notes: Strictly speaking, people from Bucaramanga are 'bumangueses'; 'santandereano' is the name for the whole department, though the analogy with 'paisa' still works. Hints 2–3 reuse facts from existing questions: ustedeo (q-6887) and culonas (q-7752). The Chicamocha image hints at Santander. The description is generic and not very funny.

questions.description: Un abecedario que no se lee: se mira y se aplaude.
questions.question: En la Lengua de Señas Colombiana sirvo para deletrear nombres que no tienen seña: cada letra es una forma de la mano. ¿Qué soy?
hints: Los intérpretes lo usan cuando aparece un nombre propio sin seña.
Solo necesitas una mano y alguien que te mire.
Mi nombre viene del griego «dáktylos», que significa «dedo».

media.credit: Uprising Man · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Uprising Man

questions.fun_fact: Casi cada lengua de señas tiene su propio alfabeto con las manos, y no son iguales en todos los países.

quality.notes: 'Dactilológico' is a specialist term that few young teens know, so it plays nearer 11 than 9. The riddle mostly checks a vocabulary word, which makes it a bit dry. The distractors use real -gráfico/-gráfico-style terms, which is good.

questions.description: En la tienda del barrio caleño hay palabras que no salen en el diccionario del colegio.
questions.question: Viene del quechua, en el suroccidente colombiano te la dan en la tienda para llevar el mercado y casi siempre es de plástico. ¿Qué es una «chuspa»?
hints: Muchos lugares ya la cobran para cuidar el ambiente.
Hay gente que lleva una de tela para no pedirla.
Es lo que pides para no cargar las cosas en la mano.

media.credit: Joe Ross from Lansing, Michigan · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joe Ross from Lansing, Michigan

questions.fun_fact: En quechua, «ch'uspa» es la bolsita tejida donde los andinos llevan sus hojas de coca.

quality.notes: 'Casi siempre es de plástico, para llevar el mercado' rules out totuma and ruana right away, so only 'mochila' is left as a real competitor. The Quechua ch'uspa is a woven bag, so mochila is slightly arguable but fine.

questions.description: Un paisaje tan verde que hasta la Selección se ganó un apodo por él.
questions.question: La Selección Colombia tiene un apodo que viene de paisajes como este. ¿Qué región colombiana es famosa por ellos?
hints: Es una región de montañas verdes en el centro del país
Incluye a Caldas, Risaralda y Quindío
Su nombre lleva el producto que da el apodo a la Selección

media.note: Foto clara de cafetales en las montañas de Colombia: matas de café con granos rojos en laderas verdes; sin letreros con nombres de lugares.
media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.fun_fact: El Paisaje Cultural Cafetero de Colombia es Patrimonio de la Humanidad de la UNESCO desde 2011.

quality.notes: The essential coffee-plantation photo is easy to find. The coffee plants make the answer clear right away, but that is the point of the question.

questions.description: Un anfitrión mundialista que se ganó un lugar especial en la historia de nuestra Selección.
questions.question: En 1962 organicé un Mundial, y en él la Selección Colombia jugó su primera Copa del Mundo. Tengo el desierto de Atacama al norte y glaciares al sur. ¿Qué país soy?
hints: Estoy en Sudamérica, al lado del océano Pacífico
La cordillera de los Andes me recorre entera
Mi capital es Santiago

media.credit: L. Honnorat/ESO · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: L. Honnorat/ESO

questions.fun_fact: En ese Mundial, Marcos Coll le hizo un gol olímpico al legendario arquero Lev Yashin en el empate 4-4 de Colombia con la Unión Soviética.

quality.notes: The Atacama clue in the question nearly gives the answer on its own, but that is acceptable at this level. The fun fact about Coll's goal against Yashin is great.

questions.description: Un defensa que en los tiros de esquina pone a sudar frío a los arqueros rivales.
questions.question: ¿Cuánto mide, más o menos, el defensa colombiano Yerry Mina?
hints: Es de los más altos de la Selección
Gana casi todos los balones por arriba
Le falta muy poquito para llegar a los dos metros

media.credit: Bo McMillan · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bo McMillan

questions.fun_fact: En el Mundial de Rusia 2018, Yerry Mina hizo tres goles, todos de cabeza.

quality.notes: Exact heights vary a little between sources (1,94–1,95 m), but the options are spaced well apart. A player's height is a rather dry estimation fact, though the fun fact saves it.

questions.description: El primo flaquito de la guadua que se fue a vivir al frío.
questions.question: El chusque es un bambú delgado que crece en los bosques altoandinos y cerca de los páramos. ¿Para qué lo usaban tradicionalmente los campesinos?
hints: Es largo, liviano y resistente, como la guadua pero más fino.
Lo cortaban y lo amarraban en haces para llevarlo a la casa.
Piensa en casas de bahareque y en cestería.

media.credit: Jason Hollinger · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jason Hollinger

questions.fun_fact: El chusque pertenece al género Chusquea, uno de los bambúes que crecen a mayor altura en el mundo.

quality.notes: Chusque's traditional uses (bahareque, roofs, fences, baskets) are broadly right. The answer is guessable from 'bamboo', but the topic is a bit dry.

questions.description: Una montaña tan viejita que ya era abuela cuando llegaron los dinosaurios.
questions.question: Soy una montaña de roca antiquísima, con paredes verticales y la cima plana como una mesa. En Chiribiquete hay muchas como yo. ¿Qué soy?
hints: Mi roca tiene más de mil millones de años.
Mis hermanos más famosos están en Venezuela, como el Roraima.
Mi nombre viene de la lengua del pueblo pemón, de la Gran Sabana.

media.credit: lubasi · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: lubasi

questions.fun_fact: Encima de algunos tepuyes viven plantas y animales que no existen en ningún otro lugar del mundo.

quality.notes: 'Cima plana como una mesa' rules out volcán and nevado, and a páramo is not a mountain at all, so the distractors are weak. A decorative image is acceptable here, since a Chiribiquete picture would show tepuis.

questions.description: Una planta de la selva que se escapó del monte y se metió en el vocabulario.
questions.question: El bejuco es una planta trepadora que cuelga de los árboles de la selva. Pero en Colombia, si alguien «se puso bejuco», ¿cómo está?
hints: No tiene nada que ver con el cuerpo de la persona.
También se dice que alguien está «embejucado».
Es lo que le pasa a alguien cuando le dañan el día.

media.credit: EgorovaSvetlana · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: EgorovaSvetlana

questions.fun_fact: Con algunos bejucos se hacen canastos, amarres y hasta puentes colgantes en la selva.

quality.notes: q-3447 also asks about lianas/bejuco, but it asks about their use as rope, which is a different fact. The fun fact touches on that use, but it is fine.

questions.description: El río más bonito del mundo no te deja entrar sin compañía.
questions.question: Si quieres recorrer Caño Cristales, el río de colores de La Macarena, ¿quién tiene que ir contigo?
hints: Es una regla para cuidar el río y a los visitantes.
Te muestra por dónde caminar y dónde sí se puede nadar.
Es una persona de la región que conoce cada sendero del parque.

media.credit: Ricardo Gonzalez Arango · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ricardo Gonzalez Arango

questions.fun_fact: Los colores de Caño Cristales vienen de una planta acuática, la Macarenia clavigera, que se pone roja con el sol.

quality.notes: Distractors are weak: police, doctor and teacher are easy to rule out. A visitor rule is a fairly dry fact.

questions.description: Una antioqueña que vuela en bicicleta sin necesidad de alas.
questions.question: Soy antioqueña, me dicen la 'Reina del BMX' y gané el oro olímpico en Londres 2012 y en Río 2016. ¿Quién soy?
hints: Compito en una bicicleta pequeña, saltando por una pista llena de lomas.
Soy de Medellín y empecé a montar bicicleta cuando tenía 4 años.
Mi nombre empieza por «Mari» y mi apellido por «Pa».

media.credit: Fabrizio Tarizzo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fabrizio Tarizzo

questions.fun_fact: Mariana Pajón fue la abanderada de Colombia en la inauguración de los Juegos Olímpicos de Londres 2012.

quality.notes: Hint 3 gives the name's first letters, which is allowed for a third hint. Shares a topic with q-7074 and q-7371 but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Una iglesia con más oro por dentro que el bolsillo de cualquier rolo.
questions.question: La iglesia de San Ignacio, en La Candelaria de Bogotá, es una de las joyas coloniales del país. ¿Qué comunidad religiosa la construyó?
hints: El rey Carlos III expulsó a esa comunidad de las colonias españolas en 1767.
Esa comunidad fundó en Bogotá la Pontificia Universidad Javeriana.
El santo que le da nombre a la iglesia fundó esa comunidad.

media.credit: Felipe Restrepo Acosta · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Felipe Restrepo Acosta

questions.fun_fact: Al lado de la iglesia funcionaba el colegio de los jesuitas, un edificio donde hoy está el Museo Colonial.
questions.concept: Iglesia de San Ignacio de Bogotá

quality.notes: The church's name (San Ignacio) is a strong clue for anyone who knows Ignatius of Loyola. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed.

questions.description: Una ciudad donde hasta las palomas tienen balcón con vista al mar.
questions.question: Estás de paseo por Cartagena. ¿Cuál de estas cosas NO vas a encontrar allá?
hints: Piensa en el clima de Cartagena.
Cartagena está a nivel del mar, en la costa.
Para ver esto tendrías que subir a un nevado.

media.credit: Dr. Thomas Liptak · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dr. Thomas Liptak

questions.fun_fact: A Cartagena le dicen «la Heroica» por resistir un largo sitio en 1815.

quality.notes: Very easy odd-one-out. The snow option is obviously different. Fine for kids.

questions.description: La mochila más pesada y más bonita de toda Antioquia.
questions.question: En la feria más famosa de Medellín, los silleteros desfilan cargando silletas en la espalda. ¿De qué están hechas?
hints: Se cultivan en jardines y en fincas.
Las abejas y las mariposas las adoran.
Rosas, claveles y girasoles son ejemplos.

media.credit: JoranL · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JoranL

questions.fun_fact: Algunas silletas pueden pesar más de 60 kilos.

quality.notes: The Metrocable query has nothing to do with the silleteros. It's safe, but a weak illustration, and the axes say photo stimulus. Distractors (dulces, plumas) are weak.

questions.description: Una iglesia tan vieja que ya rezaba antes de que existieran los relojes de pulsera.
questions.question: La Catedral de Santa Catalina de Alejandría, en el centro amurallado de Cartagena, es de las más antiguas de América. ¿En qué siglo empezaron a construirla?
hints: Es de la época colonial.
La obra empezó cuando Felipe II era rey de España.
El pirata Francis Drake la cañoneó mientras la construían, en 1586.

media.credit: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz)

questions.fun_fact: La obra tardó más de 30 años: empezó en 1577 y se terminó en 1612.

quality.notes: A dry century question. Hint 3 gives the year 1586, so it effectively gives the answer; allowed for a third hint, but very strong.

questions.description: Un edificio tan alto que podría ver venir el aguacero antes que nadie.
questions.question: El BD Bacatá, en el centro de Bogotá, le quitó a la Torre Colpatria el título de edificio más alto de Colombia. ¿En qué década alcanzó su altura final?
hints: Es una obra bastante reciente.
Para entonces ya casi todo el mundo tenía celular inteligente.
Llegó a su altura máxima dos años después del Mundial de Brasil.

media.credit: EEIM · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: EEIM

questions.fun_fact: Se financió con aportes de miles de pequeños inversionistas, en uno de los mayores «crowdfunding» inmobiliarios del mundo.

quality.notes: 'Tallest building in Colombia' is a record that can change. Topped out in 2016, which is correct. Hint 1 rules out the 1970s. A dry decade question.

questions.description: Una isla a la que antes nadie quería ir y ahora tiene lista de espera.
questions.question: La isla Gorgona, en el Pacífico, hoy es parque natural, pero antes fue una cárcel. ¿En qué década la cerraron?
hints: La cárcel cerró antes del año 2000.
Funcionó unos 25 años.
La cerraron en la misma década en que Gabo ganó el Nobel.

media.credit: AVIATUR · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AVIATUR

questions.fun_fact: Cada año llegan ballenas jorobadas a las aguas de Gorgona para tener sus crías.

quality.notes: The prison ran from 1960 to 1984, so the facts check out. Asking for the decade a prison closed is close to memorising a date. Few 13-year-olds would know it, so a 10 fits better than an 8. The question is a bit dry. It's related to q-6973 (the Gorgona prison) but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Tranquilo, que para conseguir esto no hay que pelear con ningún dragón.
questions.question: En los mercados del Putumayo y el Caquetá venden frasquitos de «sangre de drago». Es roja, espesa y la usan para curar heridas. ¿Qué es?
hints: Sale del bosque, pero no de un animal.
Si te la frotas en la piel, se vuelve una espumita clara.
La sacan haciéndole cortes a la corteza de un árbol amazónico.

media.credit: Miguernesto · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Miguernesto

questions.fun_fact: La sangre de drago sale del árbol Croton lechleri, y los pueblos indígenas del Amazonas la usan desde hace siglos como cicatrizante.

quality.notes: Hint 1 rules out the frog option early, but that's acceptable.

questions.description: Una palabra que llegó a Colombia con una mazorca debajo del brazo.
questions.question: «Chócolo» (o choclo), la mazorca tierna, viene de la misma lengua indígena que nos dio «papa» y «cancha». ¿De dónde es esa lengua?
wrong_answers: De la selva amazónica de Brasil
hints: Es una lengua que todavía hablan millones de personas en Sudamérica.
En esas tierras frías se domesticó la papa hace miles de años.
Es el quechua, la lengua del imperio de los incas, con capital en Cusco.

media.credit: Wilson, Samuel; · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons

questions.fun_fact: «Chócolo» viene del quechua «chuqllu», y en Perú, Chile y Argentina todavía dicen «choclo».

quality.notes: Quechua is spoken across the Andes (Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador). 'Andes del Perú' is a fair answer but a little narrow. It's related to q-5164 (Quechua as the most spoken Indigenous language), but this asks about a word's origin, so it's a different fact.

questions.description: Una blusa con más paciencia que una abuela haciendo fila en el banco.
questions.question: Mira esta mola del pueblo gunadule. ¿Cómo se hace?
questions.answer: Con capas de tela recortadas y cosidas
wrong_answers: Con hilos tejidos en un telar
Con pintura de colores sobre algodón
hints: Se hace a mano, con aguja y tijeras.
Los colores de abajo se asoman por los cortes de la tela de arriba.
Se ponen varias telas de colores una encima de otra y se van cortando y cosiendo.

media.note: Foto clara de una mola gunadule (kuna) de colores, donde se vean las capas de tela recortadas.
media.credit: Johantheghost · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Johantheghost

questions.fun_fact: Las mujeres gunadule llevan las molas en sus blusas, y hacer una sola puede tomar semanas.

quality.notes: A close look at the photo helps players work out the technique, which is fine. Clear mola photos are easy to find on Commons. q-5103 also uses molas but asks about the region.

questions.description: Una palabra que entró al español soplando a más de 200 kilómetros por hora.
questions.question: Su nombre viene del taíno, el de un dios de las tormentas, y en 2020 uno arrasó la isla de Providencia. ¿Qué es?
hints: Se forma sobre el mar caliente del Caribe.
Tiene un «ojo» en el centro donde todo está calmado.
El que golpeó Providencia se llamaba Iota.

media.credit: Juandareina · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juandareina

questions.fun_fact: En noviembre de 2020 el huracán Iota pasó muy cerca de Providencia y dañó la gran mayoría de las casas de la isla.

quality.notes: Tsunami is a weak distractor because it isn't a storm.

questions.description: Un abuelito barbado que con un solo bastonazo cambió el paisaje para siempre.
questions.question: Bochica fue un sabio de barba larga que enseñó a los muiscas a tejer; según la leyenda, abrió con su bastón el Salto del Tequendama. ¿Para qué?
questions.answer: Para sacar el agua que inundaba la sabana
wrong_answers: Para regar los cultivos de maíz
Para esconder el oro de los caciques
Para que los peces subieran del Magdalena
hints: Los muiscas estaban en problemas por culpa de un dios bravo.
Chibchacum los había castigado con muchísima lluvia.
Las tierras de Bogotá estaban debajo del agua.

media.credit: Felipe Restrepo Acosta · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Felipe Restrepo Acosta

questions.fun_fact: Según el mito, Bochica castigó a Chibchacum poniéndolo a cargar la Tierra en los hombros, y por eso tiembla.

quality.notes: Accurate Muisca legend: Chibchacum flooded the savanna and Bochica drained it. Hint 2 ("muchísima lluvia") already points hard at the answer. The question runs about 150 characters, which is long for reading aloud.

questions.description: Un pez con bigotes que lleva siglos nadando en el frío bogotano sin pedir ruana.
questions.question: ¿Cómo se llama el pez con bigotes de los ríos fríos de la sabana de Bogotá, que comían los muiscas?

review.feedback: The fun fact names the wrong book. Vito Apüshana won the 2000 Casa de las Américas prize for «Encuentros en los senderos de Abya Yala». «Contrabandeo sueños con alijunas cercanos» is an earlier book of his, from 1992. The description's joke about smuggling dreams also refers to that earlier book. Correct the fun fact and rework the description. Verificación de datos: wrong. The answer (Casa de las Américas, 2000) is right, but the fun fact is wrong. The 2000 prize was for «Encuentros en los senderos de Abya Yala», not «Contrabandeo sueños con alijunas cercanos». That book was published in 1992 by Universidad de La Guajira.

previous.feedback: Hint 2 ("La institución lleva el nombre de todo el continente") gives the answer away. "Casa de las Américas" is the only option named after a continent, so hint 2 solves the question as well as hint 3 does. Hint 1 (Havana) also points straight to the answer for anyone who knows the prizes, because it's the only Cuban one. Hint 1 should be vague (e.g. the prize is old and goes to Latin American and Caribbean writing), and hint 2 should not single out the option by its name.

revision.reason: Rewrote hints 1 and 2 so they no longer single out the answer by its Havana location or its continental name; Havana moves to hint 3.

review.feedback: Hint 2 gives the answer away: 'la Expedición Botánica' says outright that he painted plants, so against Aves, Volcanes and Mapas it settles the question before hint 3. Hint 2 should name Mutis or the era without the word 'Botánica', for example 'Trabajó casi 30 años para el sabio gaditano José Celestino Mutis'.

previous.feedback: Hint 2 says Matís worked 'más de 30 años' with Mutis. That is wrong: he joined the Expedición Botánica in 1783 and Mutis died in 1808, so he worked with Mutis himself for about 25 years (about 29 years with the Expedición in total). Change the hint to 'cerca de 30 años en la Expedición Botánica dirigida por…', as the fact check suggests. Verificación de datos: wrong. Answer (flowers) is right, but hint 2 says Matís worked 'más de 30 años' with Mutis. He served the Expedición Botánica about 27 years (1783–1812), and Mutis died in 1808, so about 25 years with Mutis himself.

revision.reason: Corrected hint 2: Matís spent about 30 years with the Expedición Botánica, not more than 30 years with Mutis himself.

previous.feedback: Hint 3 is wrong. Earth is about 12,700 km wide, so 8,000 km is about two-thirds of its width, not "a bit less". The fact check also returned "wrong" for this reason. hints: Nothing inside the clock gets used up or wears out.
The tick comes from something tiny that moves back and forth extremely regularly.
Cesium is the favorite choice: it does this about 9 billion times a second.

media.credit: Blervis · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Blervis

questions.fun_fact: The official second is defined as exactly 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the light given off by a cesium-133 atom.

quality.notes: “Vibrations of atoms” simplifies things: the clock really counts the frequency of the radiation from a hyperfine transition. The fun fact's “light given off” is loose too, since cesium clocks use microwave radiation that the atoms absorb. The question is long, at about 170 characters.

It can pick up paper clips.

media.author: Acabashi

questions.fun_fact: Despite the name, electrons don't actually spin like tops. Spin is a purely quantum property with no everyday equivalent.

quality.notes: The question simplifies the physics: in a magnet, the spins line up in domains. Hint 1 already points clearly to the answer. The answer_kind “group” doesn't fit this question, but that is metadata only.

revision.reason: Replaced hints 1 and 2, which gave the answer away, with vaguer ones and kept the paper-clip hint as hint 3.

questions.description: Doctors who fix a problem by shaking it to pieces.
questions.question: Doctors fire focused shock waves into the body from outside, with no cut, to shatter something into bits small enough to leave on their own. What?
hints: It treats something that can cause very sharp pain.

media.credit: Kgbo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kgbo

questions.fun_fact: The name lithotripsy comes from Greek words meaning “stone crushing”.

quality.notes: Shock waves are also sometimes used on gallstones, but gallstones aren't an option. The distractors are weak: ear wax and swallowed coins are clearly silly, and broken bones don't fit “shatter … to leave on their own”. Hint 2 (lithotripsy, from the Greek for stone) strongly points to stones. The question is a bit long at about 150 characters. A decorative hospital image is fine, but an illustrative one would also have been safe.

questions.description: A system where twelve inches make a foot and nobody asks why.

media.author: Biking Nikon Maui from Sort of near San Francisco

quality.notes: The 1824 Weights and Measures Act and the gallon figures in the fun fact are correct. The Roman Empire is a good distractor (the inch comes from the Roman uncia). q-4268 has the same answer but asks a different fact, so this isn't a real overlap. The question is a little dry, though the fun fact helps. The axes say “photo”, but the media is decorative.

questions.description: The small print on the medicine box, finally explained.

The question feels like a dry school test with little surprise, and the mosquito fun fact rescues it only a little. For 11-year-olds it may be closer to 6.

questions.description: A chart where everyone gets a box and nobody gets to leave.

questions.description: A little gadget that rides along on every trip without ever paying for a ticket.
questions.question: Look at the photo: this small device presses against a bicycle tire. What is it for?
hints: It has a little wheel that spins when the tire turns.
Riders often flip it away from the tire when they don't need it.
You'd want it most when riding at night.

media.note: A clear photo of a bottle dynamo mounted on a bicycle, its small roller touching the side of the tire; no lamp switched on and no labels.
media.credit: https://www.flickr.com/photos/23672158@N04/ · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: https://www.flickr.com/photos/23672158@N04/

questions.fun_fact: Many modern bikes hide the dynamo inside the hub of the front wheel, where it doesn't rub the tire.

quality.notes: Bottle dynamos are familiar mostly in Europe and Asia, but players can work the answer out from the roller. Commons has clear bottle dynamo photos, so the essential image is fine.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which gave the answer away by mentioning electricity, with a vaguer hint.

hints: It has a little wheel that spins when the tire turns.
It turns movement into electricity.
You'd want it most when riding at night.

questions.description: Little crystals with a big winter job.
questions.question: In cold countries, trucks spread crystals like these on roads in winter. What for?
hints: It has to do with keeping cars from sliding.
Water with this mixed in freezes at a lower temperature.
Snowy, slippery roads get safer after the trucks pass.

media.note: Close-up of coarse rock salt crystals (road salt), no text or road visible.
media.credit: Famartin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Famartin

questions.fun_fact: Salt water freezes at a lower temperature than plain water, so salt can melt ice even when it's below 0 °C (32 °F).

quality.notes: Kids in warm countries have never seen road salt, so 3 is slightly low. Still, 'cold countries' plus 'winter' lets them reason to the answer. Hint 2 is already very strong. Shares the salt topic with q-6515 and q-3886, but this is a different fact.

questions.description: A glass of water, a spoon, and far too much patience.
questions.question: You stir sugar into cold water until new grains just sink and stay at the bottom. What kind of solution is the water now?
hints: The water can't hold any more sugar.
It's “full up” with what's dissolved in it.
The same word describes a sponge that can't soak up any more water.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: Hot water can hold far more sugar than cold water, which is how rock candy is made: the extra sugar forms crystals as the water cools.

quality.notes: Mostly a school vocabulary term, so it's a bit dry. Hint 1 ('can't hold any more') nearly defines the answer, but that is acceptable.

questions.description: Some cities wear a brown hat that nobody asked for.
questions.question: It's a brownish haze over big cities, worst on sunny days without wind. What mostly causes it?
hints: Humans make it.
It often gets worse during rush hour.
Cities often limit traffic on the worst days to clear it.

media.credit: Eltiempo10 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eltiempo10

questions.fun_fact: Sunlight makes smog worse: it turns car fumes into ozone, a gas that stings the eyes and lungs.

quality.notes: The clue 'its name joins two words' adds nothing toward the cause being asked about; it only helps identify smog. Desert dust can also cause brown haze over cities like Beijing, but the 'no wind' clue points away from it. The fun fact simplifies things: ozone comes from car fumes reacting in sunlight.

previous.feedback: Hint 2 (“It comes out of tailpipes and chimneys.”) just restates the answer “Fumes from cars and factories” in other words, so it gives the answer away before hint 3. Hint 2 should only narrow things down, for example by saying that the source is something people use every day in cities, without naming cars, exhausts or factories.

revision.reason: Hint 2 restated the answer, so I replaced it with a rush-hour clue that narrows things down without naming cars or factories.

hints: Humans make it.
It comes out of tailpipes and chimneys.
Cities often limit traffic on the worst days to clear it.

questions.description: Ancient relatives who picked the hardest-to-reach room in the whole house.

hints: The name honors the cave where the bones were found.
The chamber holding the bones is called Dinaledi, the plural form of the same word.
You can see thousands of them on a clear night.

media.author: Olof Somell (Nobel Museum)

questions.fun_fact: Some passages to the Homo naledi chamber are only about 18 cm (7 in) wide, so the team chose slim cavers to dig.

quality.notes: The meaning of a Sesotho word is pure memorisation; only someone who knows the Rising Star cave can link it. That makes it closer to 14. Other 'star' answers in the pool are unrelated facts.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which pointed only to Star, with a vaguer hint about the Dinaledi Chamber.

hints: The name honors the cave where the bones were found.
The cave's English name describes something climbing up the sky.
You can see thousands of them on a clear night.

questions.description: The first dinosaurs showed up, and somebody had to come up with a name for the party.

hints: The name was given by a geologist, not a fossil hunter.
Look at the start of the word.
A tricycle has this many wheels.

media.credit: Internet Archive Book Images · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Internet Archive Book Images

questions.fun_fact: The Triassic began right after the Great Dying, so life was rebuilding almost from scratch.

quality.notes: Players can reason from 'Tri-'. 'A three-horned skull' is a good trap. Hint 2 already points hard at 'tri'.

questions.description: The best way to become famous in a million years is to lie very, very still.
questions.question: Here, dead animals get covered quickly by fine mud, scavengers rarely reach them, and layers pile up over time. Where is it most likely to make fossils?

hints: Bones left out in the open get eaten or crumble.
The place is under something.
Fish swim above it.

media.credit: BLMUtah · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: BLMUtah

questions.fun_fact: Only a tiny share of all animals that ever lived became fossils; most just rotted away.

quality.notes: "Fine mud" and "layers" make the only underwater option stand out, so the three dry, windy places are easy to throw out. A safe illustrative image (for example a fossil in rock) would work better than a decorative one.

questions.description: The only traffic jam where everyone is grinning.
questions.question: At the fair, small electric cars get their power from a metal net on the ceiling. What is this ride called?
hints: Each car has a long pole sticking up at the back.
Every car has a thick rubber ring all around it.
The name tells you exactly what you do with them.

media.credit: Dosseman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dosseman

questions.fun_fact: Bumper cars first rolled onto fairgrounds in the 1920s.

quality.notes: Spinning teacups and roller coasters are not small electric cars you drive yourself, so only go-karts is a real rival.

questions.description: Your body's biggest round trip, and every passenger wears red.
questions.question: This blood loop leaves the heart's left side through the aorta and comes back to the right side. What is its main job?
questions.answer: Taking oxygen to the body's organs
wrong_answers: Picking up fresh oxygen in the lungs
Making new blood cells in the bones
Carrying nerve signals to the muscles
hints: It's called the “big” or systemic loop.
The other, smaller loop is the one that goes through the lungs.
It brings the body what you breathed in and ate.

media.author: Chrystyna Martyniuk,Yana Kovalova, Dmytro Marchuk

questions.fun_fact: The aorta, where this loop starts, is the body's biggest artery, about as wide as a garden hose.

quality.notes: Dry school material. The answer leaves out nutrients, though hint 3 hints at them. The lungs distractor works well.

questions.description: Travelers' advice so short it fits on a napkin, and so useful it might save your trip.
questions.question: Complete the old travelers' rule for avoiding stomach bugs: “___ it, cook it, peel it, or forget it.”
hints: The first word is about water and drinks.

Heat it until it bubbles, and most germs die.

media.credit: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.fun_fact: Boiling water for one minute kills almost all disease-causing germs. High in the mountains, boil it for three minutes, because water boils at a lower temperature there.

revision.reason: Replaced the US-only word “vacation” in the description with “trip”.

previous.description: Travelers' advice so short it fits on a napkin, and so useful it might save your vacation.

questions.description: A sneeze-stopper that comes in a very small bottle.

hints: The flu virus keeps changing.
Each new vaccine is made to match the flu going around that season.
Many people get it every autumn.

media.author: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya

questions.fun_fact: Twice a year, experts at the World Health Organization choose which flu strains go into the next vaccine, one for each half of the world.

quality.notes: Plain everyday-health fact, not much surprise.

questions.description: The most polite way to avoid hugging your entire town.

media.author: https://www.nursetogether.com/

questions.fun_fact: The World Health Organization preferred to say “physical distancing”, because staying socially close to friends and family still matters.

quality.notes: The youngest kids may not remember the pandemic. Quarantine and lockdown are good, plausible distractors.

questions.description: A tiny eating machine that treats every leaf like a buffet.
questions.question: Look at this little animal munching on a leaf. What is it called?
hints: You can often find it in a garden.

media.author: Jasmine Nears

revision.reason: Hint 1 gave the answer away by mentioning legs, so it now fits all four options and the legs moved into hint 3.

hints: It has lots of tiny legs.
It eats leaves all day long.
One day it will turn into a butterfly or a moth.

questions.description: A flying teddy bear with a surprising travel plan.

hints: Think about why a furry coat would help.

media.credit: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alvesgaspar

questions.fun_fact: Antarctica is the only continent with no bees at all.

quality.notes: The Arctic bumblebee (Bombus polaris) is real. Kids could easily pick Antarctica; it's fair, and the fun fact resolves it nicely. High mountains would also fit the reasoning, but they are not an option.

questions.description: It always knows who's behind you, and it never turns around.
questions.question: What is a mirror like this one made of?

hints: It can break into sharp pieces if you drop it.

media.author: Kalle K kallek

questions.fun_fact: Long ago, mirrors were made of polished bronze or copper, and they gave a blurry, golden reflection.

questions.description: Arts and crafts, but for astronomy.
questions.question: Poke a tiny hole in a card and let the Sun shine through it onto the ground. What sky event do people safely watch this way?
hints: Looking straight at the Sun is dangerous, so this trick helps.
During it, gaps between leaves under trees make hundreds of tiny crescent suns.
The Moon passes in front of the Sun.

media.credit: Lombroso · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lombroso

questions.fun_fact: A pinhole needs no lens at all: light through the tiny hole makes an upside-down picture of the Sun, just like the oldest cameras did.

quality.notes: Nice practical fact. Hint 2 (crescent suns) all but gives it away; that's acceptable for a second hint. Shares only the eclipse topic with moons-comets-and-asteroids-12, which asks a different fact.

questions.description: Counting in a storm: the only math class with fireworks.

media.credit: th_norge · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: th_norge

questions.fun_fact: Light travels about a million times faster than sound through air.

questions.description: Boats, surfboards, hot tubs: one material, a lot of wet jobs.
questions.question: Which material of hair-thin threads covers most surfboards and small boats, and also keeps houses warm as fluffy insulation?
hints: Its threads start out as a hot, runny liquid.

media.credit: Radosław Botev · CC BY 3.0 pl · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Radosław Botev

revision.reason: Hint 2 pointed straight to glass, so it now uses the itch clue and the melting-sand clue moved into hint 3.

hints: Its threads start out as a hot, runny liquid.
That liquid is made by melting sand.
Windows are made of the same stuff as its threads.

questions.description: Some mushrooms live down in the dirt; these ones prefer a home with a view.
questions.question: Look at this close-up of mushrooms growing in shelves on a dead tree. What kind of mushroom are they?
hints: Many supermarkets sell them, often in pale gray clusters.
Each cap is flat and fan-shaped, with no proper stem in the middle.
Their name comes from a shellfish they look like.

media.author: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma

quality.notes: Identifying a mushroom species from a photo is harder than an 8: few teens know oyster mushrooms by sight. The "shelves on a dead tree" detail rules out porcini and button mushrooms, leaving shiitake as the only real competitor. The fun fact (it hunts nematodes) is great but only comes after the answer. The question itself is a dry identification task.

questions.description: Taking medicine you don't need: what could possibly go wrong?
questions.question: Antibiotics are often overused, for example for colds they can't cure. What can this overuse create?
wrong_answers: Bacteria that glow in the dark
hints: Living things can change over many generations to cope with new threats.

Doctors call the worst of these germs “superbugs”.

media.author: Adrian Daerr

questions.fun_fact: When Alexander Fleming accepted his Nobel Prize in 1945, he already warned that misusing penicillin could make bacteria resistant to it.

quality.notes: The answer repeats the question's own word "antibiotics", so it stands out. "Bacteria that turn into viruses" is weak. This is an important fact but reads like a school test.

revision.reason: Made hints 1 and 2 vaguer and gave the options matching forms, with a second bacteria option, so the answer doesn't stand out.

hints: Every time an antibiotic is used, a few tough bacteria may survive.
The survivors multiply and pass on their survival trick.
Doctors call the worst of these germs “superbugs”.

questions.description: A blob that would win any shape-shifting contest under the microscope.
questions.question: Look at the finger-like bulges this amoeba pushes out of its body. What does it use them for?
hints: The amoeba's jelly-like inside flows into them, a bit like toothpaste.
They can wrap around a tiny meal and swallow it.
Their name means “false feet”.

media.credit: Alexander Klepnev · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alexander Klepnev

quality.notes: The answer names two uses joined by 'and', while each wrong option names one, so it stands out a little. Hint 3 ('false feet') nearly gives it away, which is allowed. A clear Amoeba proteus photo is very likely on Wikimedia Commons.

questions.description: A word that suddenly turned up in every news report in 2020.
questions.question: The word “pandemic” comes from Greek. According to its Greek roots, what does a pandemic reach?
hints: A pandemic spreads across many countries at once.
Its second part, “demos”, also appears in “democracy”.
Democracy means “rule by the people”.

media.credit: Stephencdickson · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Stephencdickson

questions.fun_fact: An “epidemic” is a disease spreading in one region; it becomes a pandemic when it spreads across several continents.

quality.notes: Knowing Greek roots is school knowledge, so difficulty 5 is too low for 11-year-olds. The word is similar in most of the game's languages (pandemia, Pandemie), so it travels fairly well. 'All the animals' is the only wrong option that really tempts. Asking about word roots feels a bit dry. It touches the epidemic question q-3735 but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Mushrooms that hold hands and refuse to break the circle.

wrong_answers: Animals running in circles at night
Rainwater draining away in a ring
hints: Old European folk tales blamed dancing fairies or witches, but the real reason is hidden in the soil.
The mushrooms are only the tips of something much bigger underground.
Thin threads spread out from the center a little more each year.

media.credit: Famartin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Famartin

questions.fun_fact: Folk tales named these circles after fairies or witches, and some rings are hundreds of years old.

quality.notes: Strong question. Photos of fairy rings are easy to find.

questions.description: The Moon has no supermarket, so future explorers will have to shop in the dark.

hints: These craters are some of the coldest places in the solar system.

On Earth, you'll find it in your freezer.

media.author: European Space Agency

revision.reason: Hint 2 described the substance as hydrogen and oxygen, so it now says what astronauts could use it for.

hints: These craters are some of the coldest places in the solar system.
It could be split into hydrogen and oxygen.
On Earth, you'll find it in your freezer.

questions.description: A spacecraft that went out with a bang, exactly as planned.

hints: The mission was called DART.

The same agency sent the Apollo astronauts.

media.author: NASA/Johns Hopkins APL

questions.description: Peru's ocean runs a secret kitchen, and the fish never miss a meal.

Seafloor mud stirred up by storms
Sea level rising at high tide

media.author: PIERRE ANDRE LECLERCQ

questions.fun_fact: Upwelling zones cover only a tiny share of the ocean, yet they supply a large part of the world's fish catch.

questions.description: Some corals melt at the first heatwave; these ones ask for the sauna to be turned up.

Its name is a color.

questions.description: A reef resident that would win every staring contest, mostly because it has no eyes.

media.author: User: (WT-shared) Queensland at  wts wikivoyage

questions.fun_fact: Some brain corals can live for hundreds of years and grow taller than a person.

questions.description: The crunchy guest that shows up in noodle dishes without being invited.

questions.description: Seeds are fussy guests who refuse to wake up in the wrong room.

questions.description: Ginger's secret talent, and no, it isn't making cookies spicy.

questions.description: A gadget so small, you'll find it in the sofa cushions before you find it in an ear.

questions.description: Willows look sad by the river, but they were secretly very busy.

media.author: Gareth James

questions.description: A drum that can almost talk, if you listen closely.

Each drum has a black circle of paste in the middle of its head.
It is famous in classical music from India.

questions.description: The sense nobody lists in school, quietly doing its job while you climb the stairs.
questions.question: You can climb stairs in the dark without looking at your feet thanks to proprioception. What does this sense tell you?
wrong_answers: How far away the walls are
hints: It isn't the balance organ in your inner ear.
Tiny sensors in your muscles and joints feed it.
It's why you can touch your nose with your eyes closed.

media.credit: Carlos Martinez carlosmartinez · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carlos Martinez carlosmartinez

questions.fun_fact: Astronauts' sense of where their limbs are gets confused in space, so they often misjudge where their arms are after waking up.

quality.notes: Some definitions of proprioception include the sense of muscle effort, so 'How tired your muscles are' is slightly arguable. The astronaut fun fact is plausible, but it's phrased strongly.

questions.description: Your eyeballs have opinions, and eye doctors make a living off them.
questions.question: Faraway things look blurry, things up close look sharp, and glasses can fix it. What is this called?
hints: It's very common among kids and teens.
The eyeball is often a little too long.
People with it often need their glasses to read a sign across the street, but not to read a book.

media.credit: U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Victoria Edwards · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Victoria Edwards

questions.fun_fact: Scientists think spending more time outdoors in daylight can lower a child's chance of becoming nearsighted.

quality.notes: Hint 3 ('the name says which things you still see well') only works for some languages; it fails for Spanish 'miopía'. The question is a fairly dry definition.

revision.reason: Hint 3 only worked through the English word, so it now uses a strong clue that works in any language.

hints: It's very common among kids and teens.
The eyeball is often a little too long.
The name says which things you still see well.

questions.description: Your nose runs its own anti-dust security service, alarms included.
questions.question: Dust tickles your nose and, achoo, you sneeze before you can stop it. What do we call it when your body does something all by itself like this?
hints: Your nerves and spinal cord are behind it.
Blinking when something flies at your eye is another one.
A doctor tapping your knee is checking one of these.

media.credit: Glenn Carstens-Peters glenncarstenspeters · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Glenn Carstens-Peters glenncarstenspeters

questions.fun_fact: Some people sneeze when they step into bright sunlight, and it often runs in families.

quality.notes: It shares the reflex topic with q-4631 (the knee tap and the spinal cord), but it asks a different fact.

revision.reason: The description and hint 1 both said the action is automatic and gave the answer away, so both were rewritten.

previous.description: Your nose has a self-cleaning button, and you are not in charge of it.
hints: You don't learn it, and you don't choose it.
Blinking when something flies at your eye is another one.
A doctor tapping your knee is checking one of these.

questions.description: Chatting at the dinner table, measured with scientific precision.
questions.question: Loudness is measured in decibels. About how loud is a normal conversation?
hints: A whisper is around 30.
A rock concert can reach over 100.
It's more than 50 but less than 70.

media.credit: W.carter · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: W.carter

questions.fun_fact: Every 10 decibels more means the sound is about ten times as powerful.

quality.notes: The distractors go up by a factor of ten, and 600 and 6,000 dB are absurd, so the answer is easy to guess. Use real-world levels instead, such as 30, 90 and 120. Hint 3 almost states the answer. The question is somewhat dry.

questions.description: Your tongue takes all the credit, but it has a silent partner.
questions.question: Most of what we call a food's flavor doesn't come from the tongue. Which sense does it mostly come from?
hints: Food tastes dull when you have a bad cold.
Air from your mouth travels up to it from behind.
Try eating while holding your nose.

media.credit: CC0 1.0 · Rawpixel via Openverse

questions.fun_fact: With your nose pinched, an apple and a raw onion can taste surprisingly alike.

questions.description: A hole in your vision that your brain has been hiding from you for years.
questions.question: Close one eye, stare at a cross, and a dot beside it vanishes. How many blind spots does a person with two healthy eyes have?
hints: Healthy eyes have them too; it's normal.
It's where the nerve leaves the back of the eye.
Each eye has its own.

media.credit: ROTFLOLEB · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ROTFLOLEB

questions.fun_fact: You never notice your blind spots because your brain fills in the gap with what's around it.

quality.notes: Once you know each eye has one blind spot, the count is trivial. As a 'how many' question it's a bit flat. Hint 3 practically gives the answer.

questions.description: A face only a mother could love, and even she needs a moment.
questions.question: Look at this animal with a star-shaped nose. Where in the world does it live in the wild?
hints: It lives in cold, wet lands and marshes.
It shares its home with beavers and moose.
Look to eastern Canada and the northeastern United States.

media.note: Clear photo of a star-nosed mole showing its pink star-shaped nose; no captions or location text.
media.credit: Dan MacNeal · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dan MacNeal

questions.fun_fact: The star-nosed mole can find and eat a bit of food in less than a quarter of a second.

quality.notes: Wikimedia Commons very likely has clear photos of a star-nosed mole. Hint 2 (beavers and moose) is already very strong.

questions.description: A window you can't open, but surgeons have been swapping it out for over a century.
questions.question: It was successfully transplanted from one person to another as early as 1905, it has no blood vessels, and it's the clear dome at the front of your eye. What is it?
hints: It's the first part of the eye that light passes through.
It gets oxygen straight from the air and your tears.
Contact lenses rest right on top of it.

media.credit: You&Eyes · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: You&Eyes

questions.fun_fact: Because the cornea has no blood vessels, the body rarely rejects a transplanted one.

quality.notes: The clue 'clear dome at the front' makes it easier than 9.

questions.description: A night hunter with the ears of a spy and the face of a satellite dish.
questions.question: A barn owl can catch a mouse in total darkness by sound alone. What is special about where its ears are?
questions.answer: One ear is higher than the other
wrong_answers: They are in the feather tufts on top
They are just under the beak
They are at the back of the neck
hints: The ears are hidden under the feathers of its face.
They are not lined up like yours.
A sound reaches one ear a tiny bit before or after the other, up and down.

media.credit: shankar s. from Dubai, united arab emirates · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: shankar s. from Dubai, united arab emirates

questions.fun_fact: The “ear” tufts some owls have are just feathers and have nothing to do with hearing.

quality.notes: The answer's form differs from the distractors: 'One ear is higher…' against three 'They are…' options. Hint 3 nearly gives it away. It asks a different barn owl fact from animal-behaviour-9 and q-5330.

questions.description: Sleepovers never end with a bang, only with this.
questions.question: What often happens to you right after you see someone else yawn?
hints: It often happens when you're tired or bored.
Even reading about it can make it happen.
Your mouth opens wide all by itself.

media.credit: Jennifer C. · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jennifer C.

questions.fun_fact: People catch yawns more often from family and close friends than from strangers.

quality.notes: Studies on dogs catching yawns are mixed, so the fun fact is stated too firmly. It shares the yawn topic with heart-blood-and-breathing-9, but asks a different fact.

revision.reason: Rewrote the description and hint 1 so they no longer reveal that yawns are catching, and replaced the disputed dog fact with a firmer one.

previous.description: The only thing that spreads faster than gossip at a sleepover.
hints: It's catching, like a cold, but harmless.
Even reading about it can make it happen.
Your mouth opens wide all by itself.
previous.fun_fact: Dogs can catch yawns from their owners too.

questions.description: The playground's favorite way to make the whole world wobble.
questions.question: You spin around and around, then stop, and the room keeps turning. Which part of your body causes that dizzy feeling?
hints: This body part helps you keep your balance.
It is hidden inside your head.
It sits deep inside the part of you that hears.

media.credit: Rbrechko · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rbrechko

questions.fun_fact: Tiny tubes in your inner ear are filled with fluid, and that fluid keeps swirling for a moment after you stop spinning.

quality.notes: Very easy and not very satisfying. A playground photo could show a sandbox, but that doesn't really give the answer away.

previous.feedback: The question only works among its four options: "Which of these would NOT make you dizzy?" fits countless things in the world (a sandbox, a bench, a book…), so its clue doesn't point to the answer in the real world. Hint 2 ("which one doesn't move you at all") also gives the answer away, because the sandbox is the only option that isn't a ride. It should be redrafted as a positive question with a clue only the answer has, for example asking which body part makes you dizzy after spinning (the inner ear).

revision.reason: I rewrote the "which would NOT" question as a positive real-world question about the inner ear, with new hints and a new fun fact, and rated it 5.

previous.question: You want to feel dizzy just for fun. Which of these would NOT do it?
hints: Dizziness comes from a part of your body that helps you keep your balance.
Think about which one doesn't move you at all.
You build castles in it.
previous.fun_fact: You feel dizzy after spinning because the fluid in your inner ear keeps swirling after you stop.

questions.description: Neurons get all the fame, but these helpers finally got their moment in the spotlight.
questions.question: In 1985, a study found more glial cells, the support cells of the nervous system, in parts of a famous preserved brain. Whose brain was it?
hints: The brain was kept after its owner died in 1955.
Its owner worked on light, time and gravity.
He is famous for E = mc².

media.credit: CatBS · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: CatBS

questions.fun_fact: Glial cells were once thought to be just “glue”, which is what the Greek word glia means.

quality.notes: Einstein's preserved brain is well known, so the question is a bit easier than 11. Hint 2 also fits Newton, which is fine. The overlap candidates are other Einstein questions, but they ask different facts.

questions.description: Architects spend millions so the orchestra doesn't sound like it's playing in a bathroom.
questions.question: Concert halls tame it with soft seats and angled panels. Empty gyms and caves are full of it. Shout at a cliff and it answers back. What is it?
hints: It is sound that comes back to you.
Hard, bare walls make it stronger; curtains and cushions soak it up.
Bats and dolphins use it to find their way.

media.credit: 北京驱动文化传媒有限公司 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: 北京驱动文化传媒有限公司

questions.fun_fact: Some concert halls hang adjustable panels or curtains so they can change how long sound lingers for each kind of music.

quality.notes: Concert halls really manage reverberation rather than echo, but that is close enough. The question ends with “shout at a cliff and it answers back”, which makes this easy, so I'd put it lower than 6. Hint 1 (“sound that comes back to you”) is already almost the answer. The distractors are weak for anyone who knows what echo means. Q-0954 (the nymph Echo) and the dolphin echolocation question ask different facts.

questions.description: A word that has been in pieces since ancient Rome.
questions.question: Refraction is light bending as it passes from air into water or glass. Its name comes from a Latin word meaning “to…” what?
hints: The light path looks like it has a sudden kink.
The same Latin root gives us the word “fraction”, a part of a whole.
Doctors use a related word for a cracked bone: a fracture.

media.credit: Jeremyida002 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jeremyida002

questions.fun_fact: Light slows down to about three quarters of its speed when it enters water, and that change of speed is what makes it bend.

quality.notes: Etymology questions are a bit dry. “Mirror” is awkward as a verb option. It's easier for German players (Brechung = breaking). Q-4482 asks about refraction itself, not the etymology, so it isn't the same fact.

review.feedback: This is a base-bundle question that depends on one language's words. In German, refraction is "Brechung" (literally "breaking"), so a translation gives the answer away, the same as translating the clue into the answer's own words. Separately, the description "has been in pieces" points straight to "Break" before any hint.

questions.description: The day a volcano turned the volume knob of planet Earth all the way up.
questions.question: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was the loudest sound in recorded history. Three of these really happened. Which one did NOT?
questions.answer: People heard the blast in London
wrong_answers: People heard it about 4,800 km (3,000 mi) away
Its pressure wave traveled around the whole Earth
Sailors 64 km (40 mi) away had their eardrums burst
hints: Krakatoa is a volcanic island in Indonesia.
Even where nobody heard anything, weather instruments still felt the wave.
Barometers in Europe recorded the pressure wave, but no ear there caught the bang.

media.credit: Alexander Gerst · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alexander Gerst

questions.fun_fact: Weather stations around the world recorded Krakatoa's pressure wave passing by several times over the following days as it circled the planet.

quality.notes: The facts match the usual accounts (Rodrigues Island about 4,800 km away; the Norham Castle crew's eardrums). The correct option is the only short one without numbers, so it stands out. Players can work out that London is much farther than 4,800 km, which is good reasoning but makes it easier.

questions.description: Proof that one person's old oil barrel is another person's orchestra.
questions.question: This instrument, hammered out of an oil drum, was invented in the 20th century. In which country?
hints: It comes from the Caribbean.
Steel bands from this country play it at a huge yearly carnival.
The country lies just off the coast of Venezuela.

media.note: A clear photo of a steelpan (steel drum) showing its dented, tuned playing surface. No flags, banners or text naming a country.

media.author: Loozrboy from Toronto, Canada

questions.fun_fact: Each dent on a steelpan is hammered and tuned by hand to play its own note.

quality.notes: Many adults would guess Jamaica, so I'd rate this harder than 9. A steelpan photo could include carnival flags, but the media note covers that. The question already describes the instrument, so the media could be illustrative rather than essential. Q-3704 (Nicki Minaj) only shares the country.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which gave the answer away with “two-island country”, with a carnival clue.

hints: It comes from the Caribbean.
It is the national instrument of a two-island country.
The country lies just off the coast of Venezuela.

questions.description: The piano key right in the middle of things, and it wiggles more than you think.
questions.question: You press middle C on a piano. About how many times per second does the string vibrate?
hints: Humans hear from about 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second.
Middle C sits in the comfortable range of a singing voice, not at the edges of hearing.
The number is a few hundred.

media.credit: Puikstekend · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Puikstekend

questions.fun_fact: Every time you go up one octave, the number of vibrations per second doubles, so the C above middle C vibrates about 523 times per second.

questions.description: A trip where even a short walk needs a suit as bulky as a fridge.
questions.question: There is no air on the Moon. If an astronaut there shouts without using a radio, from how far away can another astronaut hear it?
hints: Sound needs something to travel through.
On Earth, sound moves through the air.
Without air, the sound can't leave the helmet.

media.credit: Neil A. Armstrong · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Neil A. Armstrong

questions.fun_fact: Astronauts on the Moon talked to each other by radio, because radio waves, unlike sound, can cross empty space.

quality.notes: “0 m” is an odd distance answer; “Nobody can hear it” would read better. Strictly, sound can pass if the helmets touch. Once “no air” is stated, the other three distances are easy to rule out.

revision.reason: Rewrote the description so it no longer hints at silence.

previous.description: The quietest place you'll ever visit, and also the hardest to get to.

questions.description: A brass instrument that's been rolled up like a garden hose.
questions.question: This brass instrument has about 3.7 m (12 ft) of tubing coiled into a circle, and players put one hand inside its wide bell. What is it?
hints: Its bell points backward, away from the audience.
It is often heard in heroic film music.
Its name includes a European country.

media.credit: Cbusram · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cbusram

questions.fun_fact: By moving the hand inside the bell, a horn player can change the sound from bright to soft and even change the note slightly.

quality.notes: A single F horn has about 3.7 m of tubing; double horns have more, so the fact is fine but approximate. The description repeats the coiling from the question and isn't very funny. A decorative image is acceptable, since a brass photo might show the horn.

questions.description: An invisible line with surprisingly strong opinions about your vacation.
questions.question: It zigzags through the Pacific Ocean, mostly along 180° longitude, and crossing it heading west makes you skip a whole day. What is it?
hints: You'll find it on maps, but you'd never see it from a ship.
It lies on the opposite side of the globe from Greenwich, London.
It decides which date your calendar shows.

media.credit: Famartin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Famartin

questions.fun_fact: In 2011, Samoa moved to the other side of the line and skipped December 30 entirely.

quality.notes: Solid. The 180° longitude clue together with skipping a day points straight to the answer for anyone who half-knows it. The Samoa fun fact touches q-0966 (Samoa time difference), but that question asks a different fact.

questions.description: The deeper the question, the heavier it feels.
questions.question: Air presses on you with about 1 bar at sea level. Diving in the sea, about every how many meters deeper adds one more bar?
hints: Scuba divers feel it in their ears quite soon.
Many scuba divers stay within about 40 m of the surface.
At the bottom of a 5-meter diving pool, the water adds about half a bar.

media.credit: Clotho · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Clotho

questions.fun_fact: At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, about 11 km (7 miles) deep, the pressure is over 1,000 bar.

quality.notes: Hint 3 (5 m adds half a bar) nearly works out the answer, which is allowed. The distractors are tidy powers of ten.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which ruled out three options, with a vaguer one about how deep divers usually go.

hints: Scuba divers feel it in their ears quite soon.
It's deeper than most swimming pools, but much less than a skyscraper is tall.
At the bottom of a 5-meter diving pool, the water adds about half a bar.

questions.description: Some people collect stamps; this man collected tiny electric shoves.
questions.question: In 1785, this torsion balance measured the push between electric charges. Which French physicist built it and gave his name to the unit of charge?
hints: He was also an army engineer who built forts.
His law about charges looks a lot like Newton's law of gravity.
One ampere flowing for one second carries exactly one unit named after him.

media.note: Historic drawing or engraving of Coulomb's torsion balance (glass cylinder with a hanging wire and needle); no name or caption visible.
media.credit: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb

questions.fun_fact: One unit of this charge equals the charge of about 6.24 billion billion electrons.

quality.notes: A Commons engraving of the torsion balance exists, but it often carries a caption or Coulomb's name, so it needs checking. The image adds little, so 'illustrative' would be enough. The 'unit of charge' clue does most of the work. The question is a bit dry. The wording 'One unit of this charge' in the fun fact is awkward.

questions.description: Smile! You're being turned into a very large number of tiny squares.
questions.question: A phone camera takes 12-megapixel photos. About how many tiny dots, called pixels, make up each photo?
hints: Mega- also shows up in megawatt and megabyte.
It's more than the number of people living in most big cities.
Mega- stands for a 1 followed by six zeros.

media.author: 人工知能

questions.fun_fact: “Mega” comes from the Greek word “megas”, meaning “great”.

questions.description: A unit for when your legs start asking “are we there yet?”
questions.question: How many meters make one kilometer?
hints: It's more than a 100-meter sprint race.

media.author: elfgoh.

questions.description: Someone is getting older, and the candles are doing the math.
questions.question: Look at the candles on this birthday cake. How many decades old is the birthday person?
hints: A decade is a group of years, the way a dozen is a group of eggs.

media.author: Christo

questions.description: The one night a year your bed gets robbed of an hour.
questions.question: Whole countries first moved their clocks forward for summer to save coal during a war. In which year?
hints: Cars were still rare, but electric light was spreading.

It happened during the First World War.

media.author: Chris Woodrich

questions.fun_fact: In 1784, Benjamin Franklin joked that Parisians could save candles by simply getting up earlier.

questions.description: A temperature scale that makes the weather report sound like a math test.
questions.question: On Daniel Fahrenheit's scale, a healthy body is about 98.6 degrees and water boils at 212. What does plain water turn into at 32 °F?

On the Celsius scale, this point is exactly 0.

media.author: Donarreiskoffer

questions.description: Measuring with body parts: great until someone with big feet shows up.
questions.question: This ruler has inches on one side and centimeters on the other. Exactly how many centimeters make one inch?
hints: This ruler is one foot long, about the same as 30 centimeters.
One foot has 12 inches, so try dividing 30 by 12.
It is a little more than two and a half.

media.note: A one-foot ruler showing both inch markings (1 to 12) and centimeter or millimeter markings, so both scales can be compared.
media.credit: Kaviyadharshini Selvakumar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kaviyadharshini Selvakumar

questions.fun_fact: Before 1959, the American inch and the British inch were very slightly different lengths.

previous.feedback: The question isn't international enough. Solving it depends on knowing that a yard is 3 feet, which is everyday knowledge in the US and UK but not in metric countries. The ruler only shows that a foot is 12 inches, so families elsewhere can only guess before hint 3. If imperial units stay in the stem bundle, ask something players can work out from the picture, or something about the metric/imperial link that everyone meets.

revision.reason: I changed the question to the inch-to-centimeter link, which players anywhere can work out from a ruler showing both inches and millimeters, and gave it new hints, a new fun fact and a new media note.

previous.question: This ruler is exactly one foot long. How many inches are there in one yard?
hints: A yard is roughly one big step for an adult.
First count the inch numbers on this ruler.
A yard is three of these rulers laid end to end.

media.author: Kaviyadharshini Selvakumar

questions.description: Blink and you'll miss it, but this gadget won't.
questions.question: The world's fastest runners sprint 100 meters. About how long do the best ones take?
hints: It's much less than a minute.

Count slowly from one to ten.

media.author: Ansgar Koreng

questions.fun_fact: In 2009, Usain Bolt ran 100 meters in 9.58 seconds.

previous.question: Stopwatches time the world's fastest runners in the 100-meter sprint. About how long do the best ones take?

questions.description: An alien's first snack review: five stars, would follow the trail again.
questions.question: In the film E.T., Elliott lays a trail of candy to lure the alien into the house. What's inside those crunchy candies?
hints: The candies in the trail were orange, brown and yellow.

The brand is famous for cups that pair this filling with chocolate.

media.credit: Andre Carrotflower · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andre Carrotflower

questions.fun_fact: The candy in the trail was Reese's Pieces, and their sales shot up after E.T. came out in 1982.

review.feedback: The etymology is disputed. The common explanation is „Norder neye Oog“ („Norders neue Insel“), so the ending „-ney“ mixes „neu“ (new) and „ey/oog“ (island). That makes both „Neu“ and an answer like „Insel“ defensible, and the fact check rated it wrong. Hint 3 („Gegenteil von alt“) gives the answer away. The question also opens with unneeded padding (Ostfriesland, Seebad since 1797). A niche place-name fact like this is likely above difficulty 9. Either drop the question or rebuild it around a clearly settled fact. Fact check: wrong. "-ney" (Norder-ey, ostfriesisch 'oog/ey') means 'Insel' (Aue/Eiland), not 'Neu'. Norderney is simply 'nördliche Insel'. The hints ('Gegenteil von alt') are wrong too.

revision.reason: Replaced hints 1 and 2, which gave the answer away, and fixed the reference to „im Namen der Insel“.

previous.feedback: The fun fact says the Hermannsdenkmal was the tallest statue in the world until 1886. That is false: the Leshan Giant Buddha (about 71 m, 8th century) and the Bamiyan Buddhas were taller. The record only holds for the "western world". Also, the 53 m is the total height including the pedestal, not "with the sword" alone (the figure with its sword is about 26,6 m). Rewrite the fun fact, for example: total height about 53 m with the pedestal, tallest statue in the western world until the Statue of Liberty in 1886.

questions.description: The moors get a snowstorm in June, and nobody needs a coat.

revision.reason: Made hint 2 vaguer and moved the dandelion comparison to hint 3 so the hints go from vague to strong.

hints: The plant makes them itself.
The wind carries them away, a bit like a dandelion clock.
They carry the plant’s next generation.

questions.description: A hill that has had more legends than hot dinners.

His knights sat at a famous round table.

media.author: Lewis Clarke

questions.fun_fact: In 1191, monks at nearby Glastonbury Abbey claimed they had found King Arthur’s grave.

questions.description: A building site abandoned overnight because of an early alarm call.

hints: The digger in the legend could only work in the dark.

media.author: David Howard

questions.description: Hill country has its own dictionary, and you’ll need it to read the map.
questions.question: In the hill country of northern England, which word in many place names means a valley?
hints: The Vikings brought a very similar word with them.

media.author: John H Darch

questions.fun_fact: Fell means hill, tarn means small mountain lake and beck means stream: all came into northern English from Old Norse.

questions.description: Flowers, cards and chocolates: the gift trio that works on more than one person in your life.
questions.question: Mothering Sunday is to mums as which special day is to sweethearts?
hints: It's in February.

It's on 14 February, and it's covered in hearts.

media.credit: Andy Mabbett · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andy Mabbett

questions.fun_fact: Some of the oldest Valentine's messages still around come from England, including a letter from 1477 calling someone “my right well-beloved Valentine”.

quality.notes: An easy, fairly flat analogy. Hint 1 ("February") also fits Pancake Day in some years. q-8890 is also about Valentine's Day, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: A charity record so popular it kept getting remade, like a sequel nobody could stop.
questions.question: Band Aid recorded “Do They Know It's Christmas?” again in 1989, 2004 and 2014. In which year was the first version?
hints: It was in the same decade as the Band Aid II version.

media.author: Will Fisher from Richmond, VA, United States

questions.fun_fact: Bob Geldof and Midge Ure wrote the song, and it became the UK's Christmas Number One.
