questions.description: A whole week off school, just as everyone has finally learned their new timetable.
questions.question: British schools have a short holiday in the middle of each term. In which month is the autumn half-term?
hints: The leaves are falling off the trees.
It comes about halfway between the start of term in September and Christmas.
Halloween is in this month.

media.credit: Ragesoss · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ragesoss

questions.fun_fact: Most British school years have three terms, so there are usually three half-term breaks.

questions.description: Proof that marriage is all about compromise, or about building half a house each.
questions.question: Castle Ward, Winterfell in “Game of Thrones”, has fronts in two styles because its 1760s owners couldn't agree. Which two?
hints: The house stands on the shore of Strangford Lough in County Down.
Horace Walpole's Strawberry Hill had just made one of the two styles fashionable again.
The husband wanted Greek temple columns, the wife pointed medieval arches.

media.author: Christine Johnstone

questions.fun_fact: The split runs inside the house too: his rooms are Classical, while hers have pointed arches and a fan-vaulted ceiling.

quality.notes: A great story. "Classical and Gothic" is the best-known pair of opposing styles, so a well-read player can reason it out, but it also stands out a little. "Jacobean and Chinoiserie" is an odd pairing. Few people outside Northern Ireland will know this house, so it is closer to a 13.

questions.description: A statue with excellent posture and a very nervous arrow.
questions.question: This bronze archer stands below the walls of an English castle, not far from a famous forest. Who is he?
hints: He lived as an outlaw in the forest.
His enemy was the Sheriff of Nottingham.
His friends included Little John and Maid Marian.

media.note: The bronze Robin Hood statue outside Nottingham Castle; no plaque or text visible.
media.credit: Immanuel Giel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Immanuel Giel

questions.fun_fact: The statue's arrow has been stolen so many times that it has had to be replaced again and again.

quality.notes: The photo on Commons is likely to be clear. Once the photo is shown with "a bronze archer" and "a famous forest", the question is easy, so it is rated too high at 6. The stolen-arrow fun fact is widely reported, but I couldn't confirm it. The middle-ages Robin Hood questions only share the topic.

questions.description: A Merry Man named after his dad's job, which is either very handy or a bit lazy.
questions.question: Complete the name of one of Robin Hood's Merry Men: “Much the … Son”.
hints: His father had a job found in almost every medieval village.
His father's workplace often had a big wheel turned by water.
His father ground wheat into flour.

media.credit: Ema Lee · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ema Lee

questions.fun_fact: Much already appears in some of the oldest Robin Hood ballads, written down over 500 years ago, before Maid Marian joined the stories.

quality.notes: Good same-form distractors (all trades). Players can reason towards it with hints 2 and 3. The Major Oak image also appears in middle-ages-16, but that question asks a different fact.

questions.description: Edinburgh's most loyal resident never paid a penny of rent.
questions.question: Greyfriars Bobby is said to have guarded his owner's grave in Edinburgh for 14 years. What kind of animal was Bobby?
hints: He was small, scruffy and very loyal.
He's said to have gone to a nearby café every day at one o'clock for a meal.
Disney made a film about him in 1961, with plenty of barking.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.fun_fact: Visitors rubbed the nose of his statue for luck so often that the bronze wore away and had to be repaired.

quality.notes: Guarding a grave for 14 years already points hard at a dog, so the pony, cat and goose options are weak. That makes it easier than 3. Hint 3 ("plenty of barking") nearly gives it away, which hint 3 is allowed to do.

questions.description: A line so long it's practically commuting to another county.
questions.question: Which London Underground line is red on the Tube map and runs from Epping in the east to West Ruislip in the west?
hints: Its trains pass through Oxford Circus, Bank and Liverpool Street.
It's the longest line on the whole Tube network.
Its name tells you it runs straight through the middle of London.

media.credit: citytransportinfo · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: citytransportinfo

questions.fun_fact: The Central line is about 74 km (46 miles) long, and the ride from West Ruislip to Epping is the longest journey you can make on the Tube without changing trains.

quality.notes: Dry Tube-map recall. You mostly need to live in or know London, so it may be a bit harder than 8 for UK families elsewhere. A photo of carriage seats could show Central line seat fabric, but that is a small risk.

questions.description: Groovy, baby: for a few years this little street was the coolest place on Earth.
questions.question: In the “Swinging Sixties”, Carnaby Street in London was famous around the world for shops selling what?
hints: Pop stars and young mods came here to shop.
Mods wanted to look sharp, and this was where they went.
Think of miniskirts, bright shirts and slim suits in tiny boutiques.

media.credit: Philafrenzy · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Philafrenzy

questions.fun_fact: In 1966 the American magazine Time called London “the Swinging City”, and Carnaby Street was one of the places that made it swing.

quality.notes: Hint 2 mostly repeats hint 1 (mods), so it adds little. Electric guitars could look a bit plausible because of Denmark Street, but it is clearly wrong. An illustrative image of a 1960s London street might be safe here, so decorative is debatable.

questions.description: A London Zoo resident who became a book star without ever learning to read.
questions.question: A black bear like this one lived at London Zoo in the 1920s. Which storybook bear was named after her?
hints: The real bear came to Britain with a Canadian soldier.
Her name came from a Canadian city.
A boy called Christopher Robin loved visiting her.

media.credit: Charles J. Sharp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Charles J. Sharp

questions.fun_fact: The real bear was called Winnie after the Canadian city of Winnipeg, home of the soldier who brought her to Britain.

quality.notes: The bear photo is not really essential to the question; "illustrative" would fit the role better. Paddington is a nice London distractor. Hints 1 and 2 (Canada, a city) point to Winnipeg, but you still have to make the jump to Winnie.

questions.description: Shiny steel hoods that spend most of their lives doing absolutely nothing, on purpose.
questions.question: What is the Thames Barrier in east London built to do?

wrong_answers: Stop large ships entering London at night
Keep salt water out of the drinking water
Catch rubbish floating down the river
hints: Its gates usually lie flat on the riverbed and only rise when needed.
It mostly closes during big storms and very high tides.
Without it, a surge from the North Sea could pour into the city.

media.credit: Robert Lamb · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robert Lamb

questions.fun_fact: The Thames Barrier opened in 1984 and has been closed more than 200 times to protect London.

quality.notes: The answer is a little longer and more general than the distractors. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed.

questions.description: An arch that moved house before it was cool.
questions.question: This marble arch in London was first built in the 1820s for a different job. What was it?
questions.answer: A grand gate to Buckingham Palace
wrong_answers: A gate in London's Roman wall
hints: It was designed by the architect John Nash.
In about 1850 it was taken apart and moved to the corner of Hyde Park.
It once stood in front of the home of the monarch.

media.author: Chmee2

questions.fun_fact: By tradition, only senior royals and a few military units may pass through Marble Arch's central gate.

questions.description: He stands 50 metres up, and he still won't come down to chat.
questions.question: Horatio Nelson stands on top of Nelson's Column. He was an admiral: what did he command?
hints: He lost an arm in battle but kept on fighting.

An admiral works for the navy.

media.credit: Diliff · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diliff

questions.fun_fact: Nelson's statue is about 5.5 m tall, but from the ground it looks life-size because it stands so high up.

quality.notes: "Warships" is the only sea option against three land options, so anyone who links "admiral" with the sea can rule them all out. It feels a bit like a school vocabulary test.

revision.reason: Rewrote hint 2 so it no longer says the battle was fought at sea.

hints: He lost an arm in battle but kept on fighting.
His most famous victory, Trafalgar in 1805, was fought off the coast of Spain.
An admiral works for the navy.

questions.description: A place name that's really just old directions wearing a fancy hat.

media.author: Alan Hunt

questions.fun_fact: Almost every English and British monarch since William the Conqueror in 1066 has been crowned in Westminster Abbey.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 1, which pointed straight to worship, with a vaguer one.

hints: Monks once lived and prayed there.
York has a famous one too: York Minster.
It's a place for Sunday services.

questions.description: Kneel down, keep still and try not to sneeze near the sword.
questions.question: In the UK, who has the power to make someone a knight?

This person lives in palaces such as Buckingham Palace.

media.author: Tony Peake

questions.fun_fact: The light tap of a sword on each shoulder that makes someone a knight is called the “accolade”.

questions.description: Someone has tried to sneak into Camelot without a proper invitation.
questions.question: Thomas Malory's 15th-century book “Le Morte d'Arthur” tells of King Arthur's knights. Which of these is NOT a Knight of the Round Table?
hints: The odd one out is a knight, but from a different story.
He comes from a novel written in the 1800s.
Sir Walter Scott wrote about him, in a story set in the time of Richard the Lionheart.

media.credit: Bryn Holmes · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bryn Holmes

questions.fun_fact: Malory is thought to have written much of “Le Morte d'Arthur” while he was in prison.

quality.notes: This is a solid question with nothing below 4 to report.

questions.description: The ultimate wedding present: forget the toaster.
questions.question: In 1152, the future Henry II of England married a former Queen of France, who became the mother of Richard the Lionheart. What land did she bring him?
hints: It lay on the other side of the Channel.
It stretched across the south-west of France.
Bordeaux and its vineyards were part of it.

media.credit: JackyM59 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JackyM59

questions.fun_fact: Eleanor was Queen of France and then Queen of England, lived to about 80 and was also the mother of King John.

quality.notes: A small inaccuracy: in 1152 Henry was not yet king. He was Duke of Normandy and was crowned in 1154, so calling him "Henry II of England" at the wedding is a stretch. The fun fact repeats the Richard the Lionheart detail from the question. The options are strong French feudal lands.

revision.reason: Corrected the question to say “the future Henry II” (he was crowned in 1154) and changed the fun fact so it no longer repeats the Richard detail.

previous.question: In 1152, Henry II of England married a former Queen of France, who became the mother of Richard the Lionheart. What land did she bring him?
previous.fun_fact: Eleanor lived to about 80, a very long life in the Middle Ages, and she was the mother of both Richard the Lionheart and King John.

questions.description: He's got Scotland's top job, but he never popped in for a visit.
questions.question: Scotland's patron saint, Andrew, was a fisherman, Saint Peter's brother and one of Jesus's twelve apostles. Where did he come from?

Nazareth is in the same region.

media.author: Bill Harrison

questions.fun_fact: Legend says Saint Andrew's bones were brought to Scotland, and the town of St Andrews is named after him.

quality.notes: Once the question mentions Jesus's apostles and fishing, Galilee is the obvious pick. Egypt and Rome are weak wrong answers. Greece is a fair trap, since Andrew died at Patras. The fact itself is a bit dry. It sits next to q-2990 (James, Sea of Galilee), but that question asks a different fact.

questions.description: The medieval version of “just chuck everything in”.
questions.question: I bubbled away over the fire in almost every medieval peasant's home, a thick stew of peas, beans, oats and whatever vegetables were around. What am I?
hints: I was eaten every day, often with bread.
I could stay on the fire for days, with new things added.
My name comes from the pot I was cooked in.

media.credit: TopmanJnr1 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TopmanJnr1

questions.fun_fact: Pease pottage, made from peas, is linked to the old rhyme “Pease porridge hot, pease porridge cold”.

quality.notes: Bubble and squeak comes from much later than the Middle Ages, but it still works as a wrong answer. The link between pottage and the "Pease porridge" rhyme is loose. The question is long, about 150 characters.

questions.description: Court fashion with a few loose ends.
questions.question: Medieval English kings kept jesters to make them laugh. What hung from the tips of a jester's floppy, pointed hat?
hints: You hear them before you see them.
They made sure everyone noticed when the jester moved his head.
Father Christmas has them on his sleigh.

media.credit: DeFacto · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: DeFacto

questions.fun_fact: Some jesters were the only people allowed to make fun of the king without getting into trouble.

quality.notes: The jester's cap with bells is the popular picture, and it comes more from later centuries than the medieval period. The topic is close to q-3490 (jester outfit), but that question asks a different fact. The Bodiam Castle image is only loosely linked to the question.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which described a ringing sound and gave the answer away.

hints: You hear them before you see them.
They make a ringing sound.
Father Christmas has them on his sleigh.

questions.description: Interior design with a strong hint of “please don't fight”.
questions.question: Front-bench MPs aren't meant to step over these red lines on the Commons floor. They're said to be how many sword lengths apart?
hints: The idea is that no one could reach the other side with a sword.
The rule has to be fair to both sides of the House.
Imagine a sword held out from each side, the tips meeting in the middle.

media.note: A photo of the House of Commons chamber showing the green benches and the red lines on the carpet in front of the front benches.
media.credit: UK Parliament · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: UK Parliament

questions.fun_fact: MPs still have ribbon loops in their cloakroom, meant for hanging up their swords.

questions.description: Two ships went looking for a shortcut and turned up about 170 years late.
questions.question: Sir John Franklin's ships Erebus and Terror vanished in the Arctic in the 1840s. Their wrecks were found in 2014 and 2016, helped by the stories of which people?

They are the Indigenous people of Arctic Canada and Greenland.

media.author: European Union , Copernicus Sentinel-2  imagery

questions.fun_fact: The TV series “The Terror” (2018) retold Franklin's lost expedition, and Inuit actors and the Inuktitut language feature in it.

quality.notes: The Inuit are the obvious answer for Arctic Canada, which makes it easier than rated. It shares only the answer with q-3055 (kayak), and the fact asked is different.

questions.description: A bunch of plants that has been in more pockets than a lost glove.
questions.question: The tails side of the 12-sided £1 coin shows a rose, a leek, a thistle and a shamrock. What do the four plants stand for?
questions.answer: The four nations of the UK
wrong_answers: The four seasons of the year
The four points of the compass
The four Gospels of the Bible
hints: Each plant belongs to a different place.
People pin leeks or daffodils to their coats on St David's Day, 1 March.
England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have one.
questions.fun_fact: The design was drawn by David Pearce, a 15-year-old schoolboy who won a public competition.

quality.notes: Facts check out (David Pearce, 2017 coin). With four plants, "four nations" is the obvious pick for anyone who knows the shamrock or thistle, so the distractors are easy to rule out.

review.feedback: None of the candidates shows the 12-sided £1 coin that the question names. Five are George III gold guineas and half-guineas (1778–1803), and one is a Korean War bomb photo. No new search is allowed, so this needs a manual media pick, for example the Wikimedia Commons file of the 2017 £1 coin, with either side shown (search "2017 one pound coin"). No suitable picture found for this question.

questions.description: Some people iron their shirts; some people iron their grass.
questions.question: A roller bends the grass one way and then the other to make them, and blades leaning away from you look lighter. Wimbledon's groundstaff are proud of theirs. What are they?

media.author: B. Jankuloski

questions.fun_fact: The grass in light and dark stripes is exactly the same colour; it only looks different because of how the blades catch the light.

quality.notes: The question runs a bit long. The roller and light/dark clue leads straight to stripes, and the description's "iron their grass" points the same way.

questions.description: The vegetable that turns up at Christmas whether you invited it or not.
questions.question: I'm a small green ball of leaves. I'm served with Christmas dinner in Britain, and many children push me to the side of their plate. What am I?
hints: I grow in rows up a tall, thick stalk.

I share my name with the capital city of Belgium.

media.credit: Eden, Janine and Jim · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eden, Janine and Jim

questions.fun_fact: Brussels sprouts grow in spirals up a stalk that can be almost a metre tall.

questions.description: Norfolk's most famous feathered residents have a very busy diary.
questions.question: Aylesbury is to duck as Norfolk is to which bird?

media.author: Amanda Slater

questions.fun_fact: Before the railways, Norfolk turkeys were walked to the London markets in big flocks, a trip that could take weeks.

quality.notes: Rated a little high: Norfolk turkeys (Bernard Matthews) are widely known in the UK. The fun fact just repeats hint 1. The description is weak and only vaguely related. The analogy works as place-named breed, but it's a bit loose.

questions.description: Norfolk's answer to a question nobody asked: can a dumpling go for a swim?
questions.question: Norfolk dumplings, nicknamed “swimmers”, leave out one ingredient that most British dumplings use. Which one?
hints: They were traditionally made from leftover bread dough.

media.author: Mothusi Sekhomba

questions.fun_fact: Norfolk cooks used up spare bread dough on baking day, so no dumpling ingredient went to waste.

questions.description: A Borders bread so rich it practically wears a top hat.
questions.question: This fruit bread is named after a Scottish Borders town, and Queen Victoria is said to have eaten it on a visit nearby. Which fruit is packed into a Selkirk bannock?

It's a pale dried grape.

media.author: cazalegg

questions.fun_fact: The baker Robbie Douglas first sold the Selkirk bannock in his shop in 1859.

quality.notes: Mostly sultanas, though some sources mention raisins. The Queen Victoria story is a hedged legend. It's a fairly dry regional-food fact.

revision.reason: Rewrote hint 2 so it no longer gives the fruit's size or how it is preserved, which ruled out the wrong options.

hints: It's a tea-time loaf, sliced and buttered.
The fruit is small and dried, and it's packed in so tightly that there's almost more fruit than bread.
It's a pale dried grape.

questions.description: A cat so proud of its little island that it put the island's name on its passport.
questions.question: The Manx cat comes from the Isle of Man. Because of a natural gene change, many Manx cats are born without what?
hints: It's a body part most cats have, and most people would notice if it was missing.
Some Manx cats have only a short stub of it.
Other cats swish it when they are cross.

media.credit: David Purchase · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Purchase

questions.fun_fact: An old legend says the Manx cat lost its tail when Noah slammed the door of the Ark just as it ran in late.

quality.notes: Decorative is the wrong role: an Isle of Man coast photo is a safe illustrative image. Other tail questions in the pool ask different facts.

revision.reason: Made hint 1 vaguer and replaced hint 2, which ruled out every wrong option by saying where the part sits.

hints: The missing part is something other cats use for balance.

review.feedback: The fun fact says Eddie was short-sighted, but the usual sources (Wikipedia, BBC) say he was far-sighted (long-sighted) and wore thick glasses that fogged up, so the fact as written is likely wrong. Hint 1 ("Britain's only ski jumper, so he got in easily") also comes close to giving the answer away. It points straight at entry requirements, so the only qualifying-results option stands out before the stronger hints.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which gave away what the rule was for, with a vaguer hint about who brought it in.

review.feedback: None of the candidates works: the results show a rocket sled, a rocket test track, a sea shell, a butterfly wing and sled dogs in Alaska. None shows a child's sledge or snowy British hills, and #6 shows a flat snowy field, which hints at a wrong option. Also, hint 2 (“slides down, then you walk back up”) gives the answer away almost as much as hint 3.
